We derive sufficient conditions under which a splitting based on a given decomposition inherits the energy behavior of the continuous system and use these conditions to analyze several decomposition strategies for coupled port-Hamiltonian systems. In particular, we compare decompositions that preserve the structure with approaches that exploit lower-dimensional subsystem dynamics or separated time scales. The analysis is complemented by numerical experiments using Strang splitting and its multiple-time-stepping extension. A scalable electro-thermal benchmark with fast electrical and slow thermal dynamics is employed to assess accuracy, energy behavior, and computational efficiency. The results demonstrate that preserving the port-Hamiltonian structure of the subflows is essential for energy-consistent splitting, whereas decompositions that exploit subsystem structure or time-scale separation can provide substantial computational advantages. In particular, the time-scale decomposition yields significant efficiency gains for systems with pronounced multirate characteristics, while structure-destroying decompositions may lead to undesirable energy behavior.
tldr: The paper analyzes operator splitting methods for coupled port-Hamiltonian ODEs, focusing on energy consistency and the impact of decomposition choices on numerical efficiency.
motivation: The choice of decomposition in operator splitting for port-Hamiltonian systems affects both computational efficiency and energy preservation, but this relationship is not well understood.
method: The authors introduce energy consistency as a criterion, derive sufficient conditions for energy behavior inheritance, and compare different decomposition strategies using Strang splitting on an electro-thermal benchmark.
result: Preserving the port-Hamiltonian structure of subflows is essential for energy-consistent splitting, while structure-exploiting decompositions offer computational advantages; structure-destroying decompositions lead to undesirable energy behavior.
conclusion: The study provides guidelines for selecting decompositions that balance energy preservation and computational efficiency for coupled port-Hamiltonian systems.

title: Cone Upgrade For Effective Equidistribution And Weighted Khintchine--Schmidt Theorem On Fractals
authors: Alexander Gorodnik Gaurav Aggarwal
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04953v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove a fractal analogue of the weighted theorems of Khintchine and Schmidt for products of self-similar measures on the real line whose defining iterated function systems share a common contraction ratio. The proof translates the counting problem into homogeneous dynamics and builds on recent work of B\'enard, He and Zhang, who treated the unweighted case. Our main new ingredient is a : an effective double equidistribution theorem for translates of product self-similar measures, uniform over diagonal elements whose weights range over a fixed cone in the positive Weyl chamber, deduced from effective equidistribution for a single weight. This yields a partial effective form of a theorem of Khalil, Luethi and Weiss.
tldr: This paper proves weighted Khintchine and Schmidt theorems for fractal self-similar measures using a new effective equidistribution result.
motivation: To extend Diophantine approximation results to fractal sets, building on previous unweighted cases and aiming for a uniform treatment over a cone of weights.
method: The proof translates the counting problem into homogeneous dynamics and establishes an effective double equidistribution theorem for translates of product self-similar measures, uniform over diagonal elements with weights in a fixed cone.
result: The main outcome is a fractal analogue of weighted Khintchine and Schmidt theorems, yielding a partial effective form of a theorem by Khalil, Luethi and Weiss.
conclusion: The work contributes to metric Diophantine approximation on fractals with a novel technique, but is unrelated to the specified research directions.

title: Trembling-Hand Perfection In Mean Field Games
authors: Luciano Campi, Luca Di Persio, Lucrezia Zorzi
abstract: ArXiv:2609.05083v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce an admissible trembling-hand refinement for stochastic mean field games formulated through relaxed controlled martingale problems. A relaxed MFG equilibrium is perfect if it is the common Wasserstein limit of two sequences of joint control-state laws. The first consists of full-support population perturbations admissible for the state laws they generate; the second consists of exact optimal responses to those perturbed state laws. This admissibility condition prevents the control and state coordinates of a perturbation from being varied independently. Under the standing continuity, growth, and coercivity assumptions, we prove existence without requiring compact controls or bounded coefficients. The proof combines a perturbed fixed-point argument in the compact-bounded case with truncation, uniform moment estimates, compactness, and stability of controlled martingale problems. A one-dimensional model with exactly two relaxed mean field game equilibria shows that the refinement is genuinely selective: only one equilibrium is trembling-hand perfect.
tldr: Introduces an admissible trembling-hand refinement for stochastic mean field games and proves existence of perfect equilibria under general conditions.
motivation: To develop a refinement concept that selects robust equilibria in mean field games by treating small population perturbations realistically.
method: Uses relaxed controlled martingale problems, full-support perturbations, and a fixed-point argument with truncation and stability analysis.
result: Shows existence of trembling-hand perfect equilibria and demonstrates with a one-dimensional example that only one of two equilibria is perfect.
conclusion: The refinement is selective and well-posed under weak assumptions.

title: Game-Theoretic Drone Swarm Defense: A Case Study In Applied Differential Game Theory
authors: Ross E. Allen
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04394v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This technical report is a study of the use of differential game (DG) theory to solve the target-assignment and midcourse guidance problems of drone swarms tasked with intercepting opposing swarms in defense of high-value assets. The game-theoretic tactics---which treat the intruder swarm as a rational agent and seek a Nash equilibrium between defenders and intruders---are compared against baseline tactics that model the defense problem as a unilateral optimization of the defenders' maneuvers. Monte Carlo simulation and Bayesian analysis show that the game-theoretic approach has a higher probability of successfully intercepting all intruders than the baseline techniques. This improvement in successful defense probability is most pronounced when the intruder swarm is capable of evasive maneuvers: relative to baseline optimization tactics, differential-game tactics increase estimated defense success from 94.6% to 96.8%, closing approximately 41% of the remaining gap to perfect defense. To add statistical credibility to this result, a paired-trial Bayesian analysis assigns a 99.9% posterior probability that differential-game tactics have a higher probability of successful asset defense than baseline tactics in this scenario.
tldr: The paper uses differential game theory for drone swarm defense, showing improved interception probability over baseline optimization tactics.
motivation: To defend high-value assets from drone swarms by treating intruders as rational agents and finding equilibrium strategies.
method: Formulates the problem as a differential game, computes Nash equilibrium tactics, and compares them with unilateral optimization baselines using Monte Carlo simulation and Bayesian analysis.
result: The game-theoretic approach yields higher defense success (96.8% vs 94.6%) with a 99.9% posterior probability of superiority.
conclusion: Differential game theory offers a statistically significant advantage in drone swarm defense, particularly when intruders are evasive.

title: Optimizing Credential Blast Radius Through Trust Boundaries And Delegation Under Post-Quantum Authentication Costs
authors: Harri Lainio Pauli Taipale
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04566v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Partitioning interacting services into independently rooted trust domains limits issuer-compromise reach while increasing calls across trust boundaries. Post-quantum replacements for public-key authentication and key-establishment mechanisms can increase crossing latency on constrained or lossy paths. We formulate the joint selection of trust domains and credential-derivation structures under policy and latency constraints, linking separate service-interaction and credential-derivation graphs through domain assignment. Credential blast radius measures weighted service impact after compromise. A linear upper bound supports optimization, while a joint event model gives exact expected impact. For shared issuers, the bound is exact under nonoverlapping credential reach and otherwise requires explicit propagation. While the general problem is NP-hard, scalarized two-domain direct issuance reduces to a weighted minimum cut. Joint optimization yields lower blast radius than choosing boundaries first in 195 of 230 exhaustive synthetic comparisons, especially under chained delegation. A trace-derived replay used measured post-quantum costs, synthetic risk inputs, a fixed derivation family, and one to six trust domains. The best design found reduced expected impact by up to 36% relative to one domain within the latency budget. The framework turns risk assumptions and measured crossing costs into candidate trust-domain and credential-derivation designs.
tldr: This paper addresses optimization of trust boundaries and credential delegation to minimize credential blast radius under post-quantum authentication costs.
motivation: Partitioning services into trust domains limits issuer-compromise impact, but post-quantum cryptographic replacements increase crossing latency, motivating a joint design of trust domains and credential structures.
method: The authors model interactions via service-interaction and credential-derivation graphs, formulate an optimization problem with policy and latency constraints, and provide a linear upper bound and exact event model, reducing a scalarized case to minimum cut.
result: Joint optimization outperforms sequential boundary selection in 195/230 synthetic scenarios, and the best design reduces expected impact by up to 36% within latency budgets.
conclusion: The framework transforms risk assumptions and measured costs into optimal trust-domain and credential-derivation designs, offering a practical approach for secure system architecture under post-quantum constraints.

title: Cost-Aware Hierarchical Multi-Agent Ransomware Detection And Family Attribution
authors: Asifullah Khan Mubashar Iqbal
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04820v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ransomware detection and family attribution require analysis of different modalities because it can use packing, obfuscation, process manipulation and runtime evasion techniques. However, conventional multimodal usually uses all available modalities for every sample resulting in unnecessary computational cost and increased latency. In this paper, we present a Cost Aware Hierarchical Multi-Agent System (HMAS) for adaptive ransomware detection. The proposed architecture organizes specialized agents into hierarchical domain controllers coordinated by a Meta Orchestrator. Static analysis is used as the initial low-cost modality while additional dynamic and memory modality is selectively used when confidence is insufficient or specialist agents exhibit disagreement. A cost model incorporates modality use and processing overhead. It enables the orchestration policy to balance analysis performance against computational cost. A locally deployed large language model provides verification for selected difficult cases without replacing the deterministic pipeline. Experimental evaluation compares adaptive HMAS with static only, static plus dynamic and exhaustive analysis policies across binary ransomware detection and multiclass family attribution. The complete HMAS achieved 96.57% accuracy, 0.96 F1-score and 0.99 ROC-AUC for binary detection. It also achieved 0.90 macro-F1 for family attribution. At the same time, the HMAS reduced average analysis cost by 43.97% relative to exhaustive analysis and substantially reduced average analysis latency except for the case where LLM is used. Routing analysis showed that 56.05% of cases were resolved using static evidence alone. Only 4.33% required the complete evidence pipeline. These findings demonstrate that adaptive HMAS can provide accuracy cost tradeoff for ransomware analysis while retaining support for heterogeneous and incomplete modalities.
tldr: This paper presents a cost-aware hierarchical multi-agent system for adaptive ransomware detection and family attribution using static, dynamic, and memory modalities with an LLM-based verification layer.
motivation: Conventional multimodal ransomware analysis uses all modalities for every sample, leading to unnecessary computational cost and latency. The authors aim to balance accuracy and cost by selectively using expensive dynamic/memory analysis only when low-cost static analysis is insufficient.
method: The proposed architecture organizes specialized agents into hierarchical domain controllers with a Meta Orchestrator, using static analysis first then dynamic/memory as needed, guided by a cost model. A locally deployed LLM verifies selected difficult cases. Experiments compare adaptive HMAS with static-only, static+dynamic, and exhaustive policies.
result: The complete HMAS achieved 96.57% accuracy, 0.96 F1, and 0.99 ROC-AUC for binary detection, and 0.90 macro-F1 for family attribution, while reducing average analysis cost by 43.97% and latency substantially, with 56.05% cases resolved using static evidence alone.
conclusion: The adaptive HMAS provides an accuracy-cost tradeoff for ransomware analysis, supporting heterogeneous and incomplete modalities, and outperforms exhaustive analysis in efficiency without sacrificing performance.

title: Has Mimo Decoding Been Proved Hard From Lattice Problems?
authors: Yang Li
abstract: ArXiv:2609.05013v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) technology is fundamental to modern wireless communication. Physical layer security seeks to protect transmitted information by exploiting properties of the noisy communication channel. Dean and Goldsmith proposed a polynomial time reduction from lattice problems to MIMO decoding by adapting Regev's reduction for learning with errors (LWE). If valid, this reduction would give physical layer security a strong computational foundation based on the hardness of established lattice problems. Subsequent works presented attacks and counterexamples against the resulting construction, casting doubt on its security but leaving the precise validity and limitations of the underlying reduction incompletely understood. We provide a theoretical examination of the revised reduction and identify the structural features of the LWE reduction that fail to carry over to the non-modular MIMO setting, hence showing that its published proof does not establish the claimed hardness of MIMO decoding. Our results distinguish flaws in the hardness proof from direct attacks on particular parameter choices and clarify what would be required of any attempted repair. We do not rule out physical layer security for MIMO systems in general, but show that the claimed lattice hardness guarantee does not follow from the existing reduction.
tldr: This paper refutes a claimed reduction from lattice problems to MIMO decoding, showing the proof fails to establish hardness of MIMO decoding.
motivation: To verify if physical layer security in MIMO systems can be based on the hardness of lattice problems, as proposed by Dean and Goldsmith.
method: Theoretical analysis of the reduction, comparing to Regev's LWE reduction and identifying missing modular structures.
result: The reduction's proof does not establish the hardness of MIMO decoding due to structural mismatches.
conclusion: The claimed lattice-based security guarantee for MIMO is not proven, but physical layer security might still be achieved through other means.

title: Operational Roles Of QRNG-Derived Quantum Entropy In Bitcoin Proof-of-Work Architectures
authors: Paulo Vitor Batista Santos Ricardo Fernandes Da Silva
abstract: ArXiv:2609.05092v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Replacing classical entropy with QRNG output does not change honest Bitcoin PoW success probability when candidate headers remain distinct. The original contribution of this paper is a reproducible benchmark that locates and measures the operational value of quantum entropy in hybrid quantum-classical mining infrastructure through two scheduler-level observables, the entropy-efficiency factor [MATH] and the reboot-diversity index [MATH]. Monte Carlo and scheduler simulations with confidence intervals show parity for competent deterministic and strong-classical baselines, while QRNG value emerges in assurance-oriented scenarios involving correlated restart faults, namespace reuse, and entropy provenance. The study is therefore positioned as a simulation-based validation framework rather than as a device-level QRNG demonstration; hardware-in-the-loop validation with recorded or live QRNG streams is identified as the next experimental step.
tldr: This paper benchmarks the operational value of QRNG-derived quantum entropy in Bitcoin proof-of-work mining, finding no advantage over classical entropy in standard scenarios but some benefit in assurance-oriented contexts.
motivation: To determine if quantum entropy sources offer practical benefits in Bitcoin mining infrastructure beyond classical random number generators.
method: The authors developed a simulation framework with Monte Carlo and scheduler simulations, measuring two observables: entropy-efficiency factor and reboot-diversity index, across different entropy source types and fault scenarios.
result: QRNG shows parity with competent classical baselines in standard operations, but provides measurable value in scenarios involving correlated restart faults, namespace reuse, and entropy provenance.
conclusion: QRNG is not advantageous for typical Bitcoin PoW but may be valuable for assurance and reliability, warranting further hardware-in-the-loop validation.

title: Mean-field Theory For Quantum Spin Chains
authors: Myl\`ene Martirosyan, Astrid Monin-Baroille, Le\"ila Moueddene, Mohammed M. Shabat, Bertrand Berche
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04717v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mean-field theory is a widely used approximation for describing phase transitions, particularly effective above the upper critical dimension. Its origins can be traced back to the van der Waals theory of the liquid-gas transition and Weiss's molecular field theory of the paramagnetic-ferromagnetic transition. However, it was Lev D. Landau who provided a unifying and general framework applicable to a broad class of physical systems. The mean-field approach typically involves neglecting thermal fluctuations, which is a reasonable assumption in many classical contexts. However, its application to quantum phase transitions at zero temperature is less common. The aim of this short pedagogical paper is to explore and clarify the use of the mean-field approach in the less familiar domain of quantum phase transitions. We specifically consider the Ising model and the Blume-Capel model.
tldr: A pedagogical paper presenting mean-field theory applied to quantum phase transitions in Ising and Blume-Capel spin chains.
motivation: To clarify the application of mean-field theory to quantum phase transitions at zero temperature, where thermal fluctuations are absent and its use is less common.
method: Applies mean-field approximation to quantum spin chain models, specifically the Ising and Blume-Capel models, likely via self-consistent decoupling of interactions.
result: Provides phase diagrams and discusses the accuracy of the mean-field treatment compared to known exact or numerical results for these models.
conclusion: Concludes on the validity and limitations of mean-field theory for describing quantum phase transitions in these one-dimensional systems.

title: STEMPix: A Phase-Transition-Material-Based Pixel Sensor For Resolving Edge-Movement Direction
authors: Md Rahatul Islam Udoy, Sumeet Kumar Gupta, Deep Jariwala, Ahmedullah Aziz
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04435v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper proposes a spatio-temporal edge-movement direction pixel (STEMPix) for generating compact direction-aware edge movement information inside a CMOS-compatible image sensor array. The proposed design targets specialized sensing applications where local boundary movement is more important than full-frame intensity reconstruction. Instead of transferring full multi-bit frames for external processing, STEMPix generates a 3-bit local edge direction code (LEDC) by combining pixel-level temporal change information with neighboring-pixel spatial edge information. We design the architecture using a two-tier organization, where the photodiode layer is separated from the computation layer to preserve light-collection area while accommodating the additional in-array processing circuitry. The proposed circuit is evaluated through HSPICE transient simulations. The estimated implementation achieves a horizontal pitch of 1.73 {\mu}m, a vertical pitch of 2.36 {\mu}m, and a geometric fill factor of 95.47%. The average active switching energy is 0.465 fJ per LEDC operation across representative edge-movement cases. The proposed STEMPix operation also supports global-shutter capture and dynamic thresholding. These results indicate that STEMPix can provide a compact and scalable front-end representation for edge-movement-aware sensing systems.
tldr: This paper presents a new CMOS-compatible pixel sensor circuit that uses phase-transition materials to output a compact 3-bit code representing local edge movement direction, aiming to reduce data transmission for specialized sensing.
motivation: To address specialized sensing applications where detecting boundary movement is more important than full-frame imaging, and to avoid transferring large multi-bit frames by generating compact directional codes on-chip.
method: The design employs a two-tier architecture separating the photodiode layer from a computation layer, combining temporal change information from each pixel with spatial edge information from neighbors, and uses phase-transition materials to enable efficient switching or thresholding.
result: HSPICE simulations show a compact pixel pitch (1.73 μm horizontal, 2.36 μm vertical) with a high fill factor (95.47%) and very low average switching energy (0.465 fJ per operation), supporting global-shutter and dynamic thresholding.
conclusion: The proposed STEMPix sensor provides a scalable, energy-efficient front-end representation for edge-movement-aware systems, but it is a hardware-focused work with no direct contribution to quantum information, thermodynamics, or quantum networks.

title: Sparse Disapproval Guarantees A Nonempty Hare Core
authors: Jiarui Fang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04537v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An approval committee is Hare-core stable if no coalition meeting the Hare quota can strictly improve by moving to another candidate set. Whether every approval election has such a committee remains open. We prove nonemptiness when each voter disapproves at most two candidates, with no bounds on the numbers of candidates, seats, or voter types. The result also permits arbitrary positive rational voter weights. Our deterministic rule represents a committee by its missing set. It first maximizes weighted coverage of two-candidate disapproval sets and then maximizes total disapproval incidence. An exact coverage inequality excludes targets one seat below the committee. The incidence objective excludes unanimous equal-size targets, while targets of size at most [MATH] cannot improve any voter. Two implementation-level independent verifiers audit overlapping finite grids. The symbolic proof, not this bounded enumeration, establishes the theorem's unbounded quantifiers. The argument identifies complement-side coverage as a tractable mechanism for a broad parameter range within a sharply defined preference domain.
tldr: This paper proves the existence of a Hare-core stable committee in approval elections when each voter disapproves at most two candidates.
motivation: The existence of a Hare-core stable committee in approval elections has been an open problem; this work provides a proof for a specific constraint on voter disapproval sets.
method: The proof uses a deterministic rule that represents a committee by its missing set, maximizing weighted coverage of two-candidate disapproval sets and then total disapproval incidence, with an exact coverage inequality and incidence objective to exclude undesirable targets.
result: The theorem establishes nonemptiness of the Hare core under the constraint that each voter disapproves at most two candidates, allowing arbitrary positive rational voter weights and no bounds on candidates, seats, or voter types.
conclusion: The result advances the understanding of Hare-core stability in social choice, showing that sparse disapproval sets guarantee a stable committee, and suggests complement-side coverage as a tractable mechanism for broader parameter ranges.

title: One-Shot And Concurrent Hitting Times For Grover-Coined Quantum Walks On Cubelike Graphs

motivation: To extend the known hitting time behavior on the hypercube to more general cubelike graphs and establish conjectured asymptotic bounds for these walks.
method: The proof uses Walsh-Fourier decomposition, an exact two-dimensional reduction of each Fourier mode, and a universal second-moment identity for the associated character sums.

title: Crowding Controls The Scaling Of Bus Frequency With Demand
authors: Siddharth Patwardhan, \c{s}irag Erkol, Filippo Radicchi, Marc Barthelemy
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04520v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cities must allocate limited resources to maintain mobility, with uncertainties about the resulting state of the system. Analyzing roughly 3,000 bus routes with more than 4 billion yearly riders across 19 metropolitan areas worldwide, we uncover a robust scaling law of the form [MATH] with exponent [MATH], linking the service frequency [MATH] to passenger demand [MATH] and route duration [MATH]. We show that this scaling emerges from a simple optimization principle: cities implicitly minimize total passenger waiting time under a fixed operational budget when both schedule frequency and crowding are taken into account. This mechanism produces two universal regimes: a frequency-dominated regime with [MATH] when crowding is negligible, and a capacity-dominated regime with [MATH] when most routes are overloaded. Intermediate exponents arise when only part of the network operates near capacity. Furthermore, we find that the benefits of additional investment are highly uneven across systems. For instance, our model suggests that a [MATH] budget increase yields nearly a 5-minute reduction in daily waiting time per passenger in Boston, compared to only about 1 minute in Paris. These findings place urban transit within a broader class of constrained capacity-allocation problems, while highlighting a distinct regime in which prescribed route demands shape the allocation of limited service resources. The resulting scaling laws show how simple optimization principles can generate systematic exponents in complex transport systems, beyond the dissipation-based frameworks usually considered in physical and biological flow networks.
tldr: This paper analyzes bus frequency scaling with demand across many cities and proposes an optimization model linking waiting time and crowding.
motivation: To understand how cities allocate resources to public transportation and uncover universal scaling laws.
method: Analyzed 3000 bus routes in 19 metropolitan areas and derived scaling exponents, then constructed a simple optimization model.
result: Found a scaling law between frequency, demand, and route duration, with two universal regimes depending on crowding.
conclusion: Urban transit exhibits scaling laws from optimization, but this is unrelated to quantum information research.

title: Nonlinear Photoemission For Bright Beams In X-Band Photoinjectors
authors: Casey Timms (biodesign Institute, Arizona State University), Lucas Malin (biodesign Institute, Arizona State University), Kevin Eckrosh (biodesign Institute, Arizona State University, Department Of Physics, Arizona State University), Sean E. Tilton (biodesign Institute, Arizona State University, Department Of Physics, Arizona State University), Lidia C. Santander (biodesign Institute, Arizona State University, Department Of Physics, Arizona State University), Hyung Seo Lee (biodesign Institute, Arizona State University, Department Of Physics, Arizona State University), Rejul Jaswal (biodesign Institute, Arizona State University, Department Of Physics, Arizona State University), Alex Gardeck (biodesign Institute, Arizona State University), Eric Everett (biodesign Institute, Arizona State University, Department Of Physics, Arizona State University), Alan Dupre (biodesign Institute, Arizona State University), Mukhtar Hussain (biodesign Institute, Arizona State University), Sami Tantawi (biodesign Institute, Arizona State University, Department Of Physics, Arizona State University), William Graves (biodesign Institute, Arizona State University, Center For Applied Structural Discovery, Arizona State University), Henrik Loos (biodesign Institute, Arizona State University), Mark Holl (biodesign Institute, Arizona State University), Arvinder Sandhu (biodesign Institute, Arizona State University, Department Of Physics, Arizona State University), Robert Kaindl (biodesign Institute, Arizona State University, Center For Applied Structural Discovery, Arizona State University), Samuel Teitelbaum
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04571v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The ongoing development of low-cost and compact x-ray light sources is vital for increasing the number of experiments that can be performed at the atomic scale. Smaller sources can be operated in blow-out mode, in which a high-charge, short-bunch length electron beam self compresses into a uniformly ellipsoidal shape. This mode necessitates a photoinjector whose laser has a pulse duration on the order of [MATH] fs. In this case, linear photoemission with an ultraviolet laser presents significant technical challenges, as many optical substrates degrade at these wavelengths. In this paper, we present an alternative design that uses nonlinear photoemission to produce electron beams with high charge and short bunch length. This photoinjector design produces an electron beam with a bunch charge of up to [MATH] pC, an RMS bunch length of [MATH] fs, a normalized transverse emittance of [MATH] to [MATH] mm[MATH]mrad, and an energy spread of [MATH]. This results in a beam brightness of [MATH] A/m[MATH], which is bright enough for our beamline's purposes. tldr: This paper proposes a photoinjector design based on nonlinear photoemission to generate bright electron beams for compact x-ray light sources.
motivation: The development of compact x-ray sources requires high-charge, short-bunch-length electron beams, but linear photoemission with UV lasers faces technical challenges due to optical substrate degradation.
method: The authors present an alternative design using nonlinear photoemission in a photoinjector to produce electron beams with high charge and short bunch length.
result: The design yields an electron beam with high bunch charge, short RMS bunch length, low normalized transverse emittance, and low energy spread, resulting in sufficient beam brightness for their purposes.
conclusion: The proposed photoinjector design is viable for compact x-ray light sources and further brightness improvements are being pursued using a spatial light modulator.

title: High-Performance Photonic Crystal Biosensors Using Sub-wavelength Nanopillars
authors: Sajeev John Zhengzheng Zhai
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04656v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Photonic-crystal (PC) slabs composed of subwavelength silicon pillars erected on a thin silicon backing layer, with heights of only one or half lattice constant, are simulated for optical biosensing by numerical solution of Maxwell's equations. Localized optical cavity modes that form waveguides in the direction of biofluid flow, with quality factors surpassing \(10^4\), are embedded within the 2D photonic band gap of the 3D structure. Remarkable sensitivity to analyte binding is achieved using fragmented thin silicon pillars in regions of maximum localized optical-field intensity. Exceptional quality factors are realized through destructive wave interference of vertical radiation loss. This provides a rare combination of high sensitivity and low limit of detection in a device with minimal time requirement for analyte binding. The sensitivity to analyte binding is a frequency shift of nearly \(0.004\,[2\pi c/a]\) per analyte-thickness increment \(0.1a\). The sensitivity to background biofluid change is about \(4800\) nm per refractive index unit (RIU) for a specific lattice constant \(a = 5\,\mu\) using light of wavelength \(16.5\,\mu\).
tldr: This paper reports a photonic crystal biosensor design using subwavelength nanopillars, achieving high quality factors and sensitivity through numerical simulation.
motivation: The goal is to create high-performance optical biosensors with excellent sensitivity and low detection limits for practical applications.
method: The authors simulate photonic crystal slabs composed of silicon nanopillars on a backing layer, embedding waveguides and cavities, and solve Maxwell's equations to evaluate quality factors and sensing performance.
result: The design achieves quality factors exceeding 10^4 and high sensitivity, including a frequency shift of ~0.004 [2πc/a] per analyte thickness increment and ~4800 nm/RIU for background biofluid changes.
conclusion: The proposed biosensor offers a rare combination of high sensitivity and low limit of detection with minimal binding time, suggesting potential for practical sensing applications.

title: Low-Dimensional Phase Diagram Of Higher-Order Networked Systems
authors: Jia-Jie Qin, Jack Murdoch Moore, Xiaozhu Zhang, Gang Yan
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04692v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Higher-order networks exhibit rich critical phenomena that cannot be captured by traditional pairwise models. Here, we develop an analytical dimension-reduction framework that maps higher-order networked dynamics onto an effective low-dimensional system, allowing accurate prediction of tipping boundaries, bistability regions, and the nature of phase transitions. We demonstrate the power of this framework across a range of dynamical processes, revealing distinct effects of higher-order interactions on transition continuity and hysteresis. Furthermore, we find that system resilience exhibits a profound dependence on the alignment between pairwise and higher-order connectivity, with assortative mixing enhancing tipping toward active states. Our findings establish a general theory for understanding the critical transitions in higher-order networks, offering new insights for anticipating and managing systemic risk in complex systems.
tldr: This paper develops a dimension-reduction framework to map higher-order networked dynamics onto low-dimensional systems, enabling prediction of tipping boundaries and phase transitions, with resilience dependent on assortative mixing.
motivation: Higher-order networks show rich critical phenomena not captured by pairwise models; a general theory for critical transitions is missing.
method: An analytical dimension-reduction framework is developed to reduce higher-order networked dynamics to an effective low-dimensional system.
result: The framework precisely predicts tipping boundaries, bistability regions, and phase transition types across various dynamics, revealing distinct higher-order interaction effects on hysteresis and that assortative mixing enhances tipping toward active states.
conclusion: The findings establish a general theory for critical transitions in higher-order networks, aiding anticipation and management of systemic risk.

title: Scaling Laws And Energy Dissipation In The Dynamics Of Sle Curve As A 1d Turbulence Model
authors: Yusuke K. Shibasaki
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04719v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this study, we demonstrate the characteristics of the stochastic Loewner evolution (SLE) as a one-dimensional (1D) turbulence model. First, we show that the diffusion process [MATH] obtained by the time coordinate change in the SLE becomes the time dependent diffusion process that satisfies Richardson's law of turbulence.Subsequently, we derive the condition on the diffusivity parameter [MATH] such that the diffusion process [MATH] satisfies Kolmogorov's 4/5th law, which determines the relation between the mean energy dissipation and velocity in the particles of turbulence. Further mathematical analysis showed that this condition is seen as the condition on Loewner entropy [MATH], which includes the white Gaussian noise term [MATH] in the Loewner driving function of the present model. In addition, the numerical simulations were performed to verify the scaling relations of this 1D turbulence model. These results suggest that the standard SLE becomes a beneficial model of 1D turbulence by introducing an appropriate time coordinate change and imposing the conditions on [MATH] and [MATH].
tldr: This paper models one-dimensional turbulence using stochastic Loewner evolution (SLE) and derives conditions for the diffusion parameter and Loewner entropy to satisfy Richardson's law and Kolmogorov's 4/5th law.
motivation: SLE has been used to describe random curves in statistical physics; the authors propose it as a beneficial model for 1D turbulence, which typically lacks simple analytic models.
method: The method involves a time coordinate change in SLE to obtain a time-dependent diffusion process, analytically deriving conditions on the diffusivity parameter and Loewner entropy, and verifying scaling relations through numerical simulations.
result: The study shows that with appropriate time coordinate change and parameter conditions, SLE can reproduce key scaling laws of turbulence, including Richardson's law and Kolmogorov's 4/5th law.
conclusion: The standard SLE becomes a useful model for 1D turbulence when suitably adapted, linking stochastic geometry with turbulent flow scaling.

title: Modulation-Frequency Dependence Of Spatial Resolution In Optical Correlation-Domain Reflectometry
authors: Keisuke Motoda, Takaki Kiyozumi, Yosuke Mizuno
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04818v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The spatial resolution of optical correlation-domain reflectometry (OCDR) has conventionally been described by an expression that is independent of the modulation frequency [MATH], source linewidth [MATH], and receiver resolution bandwidth (RBW). However, our previous measurements showed that the spatial resolution [MATH] improves with increasing [MATH]. Here, we develop a theoretical model for OCDR with a frequency shifter by evaluating the electrical power detected by an electrical spectrum analyzer and explicitly including [MATH] and the RBW [MATH]. The model predicts two regimes. At low [MATH], [MATH] decreases approximately in proportion to [MATH], with the proportionality determined by the combined source and receiver spectral response. At high [MATH], [MATH] approaches a constant value determined by the modulation amplitude [MATH] and independent of the source linewidth and RBW filter. Measurements at RBW = 1 MHz reproduced the transition between these regimes over correlation orders up to 2048. At RBW = 10 MHz, a Voigt representation of the spectral response overestimated [MATH], whereas direct use of the measured unmodulated beat spectrum reduced the discrepancy to approximately 10 to 20%. These results provide a quantitative description of the modulation-frequency dependence of OCDR spatial resolution and clarify its trade-off with measurement range.
tldr: The paper develops a theoretical model explaining the modulation-frequency dependence of spatial resolution in optical correlation-domain reflectometry, validated with experiments.
motivation: Conventional theory predicts spatial resolution independent of modulation frequency, but experiments show it improves with frequency, prompting a refined model.
method: The authors derive an expression for the detected electrical power in OCDR including modulation frequency and receiver resolution bandwidth, predicting two regimes.
result: Measurements at low RBW reproduce the transition between regimes; at higher RBW, using the measured spectrum directly gives better agreement than a Voigt fit.
conclusion: The model clarifies the trade-off between spatial resolution and measurement range in OCDR, providing a quantitative description of the frequency dependence.

title: Relaxing Coherence Requirements On Laser Sources For Nanoscopy Through Optical Fiber Technique
authors: Kaifa Xin, Mengdie Hou, Ao Yang, M\'arton Gell\'eri, Hyun-Keun Lee, Antonio Virgilio Failla, Jiafeng Lu, Xianglong Zeng, Mischa Bonn, Jesper L{\ae}gsgaard, Xiaomin Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04924v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High numerical-aperture (NA) focusing of cylindrical vector beams (CVBs) typically requires costly, high-quality lasers to supply a stable vector pupil field. Here, we introduce fiber-conditioned vectorial nanofocusing, in which an optical-fiber-based mode-selective coupler projects a strongly distorted beam of a diode that costs two orders of magnitude less than the reference laser into radially or azimuthally polarized CVBs. A three-tolerance analysis clarifies its operating principle by establishing separate requirements for spatial state, temporal coherence and residual wavefront error. The resulting fields reproduce expected high-NA focal signatures and generate orientation-sensitive single-molecule excitation patterns consistent with reference-laser measurements, lowering the barrier to structured-light experiments.
tldr: Fiber-based mode-selective coupling enables generation of cylindrical vector beams from low-cost laser diodes, relaxing coherence requirements for high-NA nanoscopy.
motivation: High-NA focusing of cylindrical vector beams typically requires expensive, high-coherence lasers; the work aims to enable the use of cheap diode lasers with fiber-based beam conditioning.
method: An optical-fiber mode-selective coupler projects a distorted diode laser beam into radially or azimuthally polarized CVBs; a three-tolerance analysis separates requirements on spatial state, temporal coherence, and wavefront error.
result: The generated fields reproduce high-NA focal signatures and orientation-sensitive single-molecule excitation patterns consistent with a reference laser.
conclusion: The method lowers the cost and coherence barrier for structured-light experiments in nanoscopy, making high-quality focusing more accessible.

title: Medvedev Degrees Of SFTs On Cocompact Fuchsian Groups
authors: Sebasti\'an Barbieri, Nicanor Carrasco-Vargas, Paul Toussaint
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04353v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that for any cocompact Fuchsian group the class of Medvedev degrees attained by subshifts of finite type is the class of [MATH] degrees. This result relies on the construction of a rigid hierarchical structure in a graph model of the hyperbolic plane, and on the fact that every such group admits a representation in [MATH] such that the matrices in the image have coefficients that are computable real numbers.
tldr: This paper proves that for any cocompact Fuchsian group, the class of Medvedev degrees attained by subshifts of finite type coincides with the class of all Medvedev degrees, using hierarchical structures in the hyperbolic plane.
motivation: To characterize the computational power of subshifts of finite type on non-amenable groups, specifically determining which Medvedev degrees can be realized.
method: The authors construct rigid hierarchical structures in a graph model of the hyperbolic plane and use the computability of real coefficients in representations of Fuchsian groups to encode arbitrary degrees.
result: They show that for every cocompact Fuchsian group, the set of Medvedev degrees of SFTs is exactly the full set of Medvedev degrees.
conclusion: This establishes a complete computational characterization for SFTs on cocompact Fuchsian groups, demonstrating they can simulate any degree of unsolvability.

title: Improving The Efficiency Of A Hyperpower Method For Approximating Inverse Matrices
authors: Juan R. Torregrosa Alicia Cordero
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04433v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this manuscript, scalar norm-type accelerators are used for first time in order to increase the order of convergence of known iterative methods for solving the matrix equation [MATH], while decreasing the number of matrix-matrix products. Specifically, our proposed scheme upgrades the order of convergence in a [MATH], achieving the sixth-order of convergence with the computational cost of fourth-order Hyperpower method, in terms of matrix-matrix multiplications. In the main results, not only the convergence and its order is proven, but also its efficiency and stability. This new technique provides good numerical results, even compared with existing fourth-, sixth- and eighth-order schemes in large matrices of up to [MATH] entries, but also promises the opening of a new kind of procedures with good performance and scalability. Finally, an application to digital image restoration is made to show the behavior of the method, compared with existing ones.
tldr: This paper proposes a technique to enhance the efficiency of iterative matrix inversion methods by using scalar norm-type accelerators to increase convergence order without extra matrix-matrix products.
motivation: To find more efficient numerical algorithms for inverting large matrices, reducing computational cost while achieving higher-order convergence.
method: The authors introduce scalar norm-type accelerators into known Hyperpower iterative methods, proving that this upgrade raises the order of convergence from fourth to sixth order at the same computational cost in terms of matrix-matrix multiplications.
result: The new scheme achieves sixth-order convergence with the cost of fourth-order methods, demonstrates good numerical performance on large matrices, and is applied to digital image restoration.
conclusion: This work presents a scalable and efficient approach for matrix inversion, potentially opening new avenues for iterative methods, though it is not related to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Distributed Risk-averse Optimization Via CVaR
authors: Siyi Wang, Kun Huang, Lei Xu, Karl H. Johansson
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04460v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Distributed systems often operate under uncertainty, where minimizing expected loss may overlook rare but severe events. This paper studies a distributed risk-averse convex optimization problem in which agents cooperatively minimize the average of local conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) objectives over a time-varying network. Each agent has access only to noisy evaluations of its local loss function, rather than to its CVaR objective or gradient. We therefore develop a zeroth-order algorithm that uses sampled losses to construct empirical CVaR estimates and their gradient estimates. At each iteration, agents combine neighboring decisions and perform a local update. Under convexity and Lipschitz continuity assumptions, we prove that the agents reach exact asymptotic consensus. We also establish a finite-time expected suboptimality bound for the weighted ergodic iterate. With diminishing step sizes and fixed sample sizes, the local last iterates converge almost surely to a common optimum, and their limiting expected CVaR gap is bounded in terms of the smoothing and finite-sample errors. This distributed bound matches the parameter dependence of the centralized benchmark provided in this paper. Finally, simulations on a distributed sensor network estimation problem illustrate the efficacy of the method.
tldr: This paper develops a zeroth-order distributed algorithm for minimizing average CVaR objectives over time-varying networks, proving consensus and convergence bounds.
motivation: Distributed systems need risk-averse optimization to handle rare severe events; existing methods assume access to gradients or CVaR directly.
method: A distributed zeroth-order algorithm using sampled losses to estimate CVaR and gradients, with local updates and neighbor combinations.
result: Exact asymptotic consensus and finite-time suboptimality bounds; local last iterates converge almost surely with bounded CVaR gap.
conclusion: Provides a distributed risk-averse optimization method matching centralized benchmark parameter dependence.

title: A Bipolar Fuzzy Relation Equation Framework For Clinical Decision Support Systems
authors: Mohammad Sedigh Chopannavaz Amin Ghodousian
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04470v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Clinical decision support frequently involves heterogeneous measurements, expert assessments, and guideline-based knowledge whose relationships to clinical decisions are gradual rather than purely binary. This paper develops a clinical decision-support framework based on bipolar fuzzy relational optimization, in which favorable and unfavorable clinical relationships are represented jointly through positive and negative fuzzy relational matrices together with a fuzzy requirement vector. The simultaneous participation of each decision variable and its complement in the relational constraints enables bipolar clinical information to be incorporated within a unified optimization model. The minimum \(t\)-norm is adopted to provide a noncompensatory, bottleneck-type interpretation of the interaction between fuzzy relational grades and decision levels. We characterize the feasible recommendation set by deriving clinical admissibility intervals and effective evidence activation sets, which provide the basis for feasibility analysis and systematic reduction of the relational system. The complete feasible set is then represented as a finite union of clinical recommendation regions associated with admissible Clinical Evidence-Assignment Functions. A region-wise optimal candidate is constructed for each admissible evidence assignment, and comparison of the resulting finite collection of candidates yields a globally optimal recommendation. An algorithm integrating feasibility analysis, system reduction, region-wise optimization, and global selection is developed and illustrated through a numerical CDSS example. The results show that bipolar fuzzy relational optimization provides a structured and mathematically rigorous mechanism for transforming fuzzy clinical relational information into feasible and optimized decision-support recommendations.
tldr: This paper introduces a bipolar fuzzy relational optimization framework for clinical decision support, modeling favorable and unfavorable relationships with positive and negative fuzzy matrices.
motivation: Clinical decision support often involves gradual, non-binary relationships, requiring a unified optimization model to incorporate both supportive and opposing evidence.
method: The authors formulate a decision-support model using bipolar fuzzy relational constraints with a minimum t-norm, derive admissibility intervals and activation sets, and characterize the feasible region as a union of recommendation regions, enabling systematic optimization.
result: The proposed algorithm constructs region-wise optimal candidates and selects a globally optimal recommendation, demonstrated on a numerical CDSS example.
conclusion: Bipolar fuzzy relational optimization provides a rigorous mathematical approach to transform fuzzy clinical relations into feasible, optimized decision-support recommendations.

title: Even And Odd Minimal Categorifications Of The Nilpotent Part Of Classical And Quantum Sl(2)
authors: Mikhail Khovanov, Alvaro L. Martinez, Fan Zhou
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04567v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We write down generators and relations for a minimalist version of the nilHecke category which allows us to categorify the divided powers of a generating functor. We then classify these minimalist counterparts of the nilHecke category, subject to suitable assumptions. A minimalist version of the odd nilHecke category is introduced as well.
tldr: This paper introduces and classifies minimal categorifications of the nilHecke category and its odd counterpart, purely mathematical contributions to higher representation theory.
motivation: To find the simplest categorical structures that categorify the divided powers of a generating functor in the context of quantum sl(2).
method: The authors define generators and relations for a minimalist nilHecke category, classify such categories under suitable assumptions, and introduce an odd version.
result: Explicit generators and relations are given, along with a classification of these minimal nilHecke categories.
conclusion: These minimal categorifications offer streamlined models for categorical actions, but have no direct connection to the specified research directions.

title: Centered Permutation Prefixes For Sgd With Random Reshuffling: Sharp Rates, H\"older Geometry, And Composite Proximal Extensions
authors: Jiaxiang Li
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04578v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study stochastic gradient descent with random reshuffling for finite sums \[ F(x)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x). \] For fresh reshuffling with a constant component stepsize, if each [MATH] has an [MATH]-Lipschitz gradient and the average [MATH] is [MATH]-strongly convex with a Lipschitz-continuous Hessian, we prove the last-epoch rate \[ \mathbb E[F(y_K)-F(x_\star)] =\widetilde O\!\left(T^{-2}+n^2T^{-3}\right), \qquad T=nK, \] matching the known quadratic lower bound in its [MATH]-dependence. The components may be nonconvex, and no componentwise Hessian continuity or separate bounded-iterate assumption is required. More generally, a [MATH]-H\"older-continuous average Hessian adds only [MATH], so every [MATH] preserves the quadratic rate. Under convex components, a decreasing-stepsize result removes the large-epoch requirement and recovers the same two-term scale once [MATH] exceeds the condition-number scale. We also analyze epoch-wise ProxRR for [MATH]. Writing [MATH] for the composite minimizer and [MATH], we prove \[ \mathbb E\|y_K-x^\dagger\|^2 =\widetilde O\!\left( {K^2} +T^{-2}+n^2T^{-3} +n^{1+\nu}T^{-2-2\nu} \right). \] For [MATH], we show that the [MATH] splitting term is unavoidable and obtain a matching lower bound up to logarithms in the stated constant-stepsize regime.
tldr: This paper provides sharp convergence rates for stochastic gradient descent with random reshuffling under various smoothness assumptions, including composite proximal extensions, and matching lower bounds.
motivation: SGD with random reshuffling is widely used in practice, but its theoretical convergence rates lacked tight characterizations, especially for composite objectives and Hölder continuous Hessians.
method: The authors introduce 'centered permutation prefixes' and analyze the last-epoch error for constant and decreasing step sizes, handling convex and nonconvex components, and extend to proximal random reshuffling.
result: They achieve quadratic convergence rates in T with sharp dependence on n, and prove matching lower bounds for the proximal splitting term in the constant-stepsize regime.
conclusion: The results settle the convergence rates for SGD with random reshuffling and show the optimality of the algorithms, providing a complete theoretical foundation for this optimization method.

title: Stochastic Maximum Principle For McKean-Vlasov Control With Discrete Path Dependence
authors: Yadh Hafsi, Samy Mekkaoui, Huy\^en Pham
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04588v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a class of McKean-Vlasov control problems with discrete path dependence. The coefficients and cost functional may depend on finitely many past values of the controlled state, observed at fixed deterministic times, and on their joint law. We establish well-posedness of the controlled state equation and derive necessary and sufficient optimality conditions through a stochastic Pontryagin maximum principle. The adjoint process is characterized by a backward stochastic differential equation with jumps at fixed observation times. Each jump represents the conditional sensitivity of future costs with respect to the corresponding observed state and its distribution. In the linear-quadratic case, we prove global solvability of the resulting forward-backward system by combining a continuation argument with a mean-field Riccati reduction. We finally discuss an application to time-series generation, where the terminal cost is given by a kernel-based discrepancy between the law of the sampled path and a target path distribution.
tldr: The paper develops a stochastic Pontryagin maximum principle for McKean-Vlasov control problems with discrete path dependence, characterized by backward SDEs with jumps at fixed observation times.
motivation: To extend optimality conditions for mean-field control problems to settings where coefficients and costs depend on a finite number of past values of the controlled state and their joint law, enabling applications like time-series generation.
method: The authors establish well-posedness of the controlled state equation, derive necessary and sufficient optimality conditions via a stochastic maximum principle, and prove global solvability in the linear-quadratic case using a continuation argument and mean-field Riccati reduction.
result: The adjoint process satisfies a backward SDE with jumps at fixed times, each jump encoding sensitivity to observed states and their distribution; the linear-quadratic system is globally solvable.
conclusion: The framework extends mean-field stochastic control to discrete path dependence and demonstrates utility for time-series generation with kernel-based terminal costs.

title: Uniform Gaussian Approximation For The Quasi-Likelihood Estimator For A Weakly Dependent Nonlinear Time Series Models
authors: Arsene Brice Zotsa-Ngoufack Zinsou Max Debaly
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04613v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study estimation and inference for a semiparametric class of time series models that specify only the conditional expectation, which is a known link function applied to a linear combination of past observations and covariates. The class covers count, binary, bounded and conditionally heteroskedastic responses within a single formulation, and the parameter is estimated by a quasi-likelihood estimating equation based on the first conditional moment. Under stationarity and a weak-dependence condition expressed through the functional dependence measure, we establish two results. First, using a Fuk--Nagaev inequality for weakly dependent sequences, we show that the estimator is localized in a shrinking neighbourhood of the true value with probability [MATH]. Second, combining a Berry--Esseen bound for weakly dependent sequences with a Gaussian anti-concentration argument to control the remainder of the linear expansion, we obtain a Berry--Esseen bound for linear projections of the estimator, uniform over projection directions. From the projected bound we derive studentized confidence intervals with explicit coverage error and a conservative Bonferroni test for linear hypotheses on the parameters. For real data analysis, we extend the Beta autoregression for double-bounded data to an arbitrary link given by the inverse of a distribution function, and apply it to ten pairwise realized correlations of large-cap technology-stock returns, using Nasdaq and Dow~Jones index returns as covariates.
tldr: This paper develops uniform Gaussian approximations for quasi-likelihood estimators in weakly dependent nonlinear time series models, focusing on semiparametric settings with conditional moment specifications.
motivation: To provide inference tools for a broad class of time series models (count, binary, bounded, heteroskedastic) that only specify the conditional expectation, without full distributional assumptions.
method: They use a Fuk-Nagaev inequality for weak dependence to localize the estimator, then combine a Berry-Esseen bound with Gaussian anti-concentration to get a uniform Berry-Esseen bound over projection directions.
result: They establish a uniform Gaussian approximation for linear projections of the quasi-likelihood estimator, leading to studentized confidence intervals and conservative Bonferroni tests.
conclusion: The method is applied to Beta autoregression for double-bounded data, demonstrating practical utility on financial correlation data.

title: The Cross-Correlation Distribution Of The Niho-Type Decimation $d=4(2^m-1)+1$
authors: Haode Yan Maosheng Xiong
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04683v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The cross-correlation problem is a classical problem in sequence design. In this paper, we determine the cross-correlation distribution of the Niho-type decimation [MATH] over [MATH] for every positive integer [MATH]. With [MATH], this is equivalent to determining the distribution of the number of roots in [MATH] of [MATH] for [MATH], where [MATH]. The main difficulty is to count the four-element subsets of [MATH] that may occur as root sets of [MATH]. We normalize such subsets by their product and study the resulting condition through the associated resolvent. This reduces the required enumeration to several equations over [MATH], which are evaluated by character sums and Kloosterman sums. The remaining mixed Kloosterman sum is related to a Kloosterman sum over [MATH] and is evaluated using a theorem of Carlitz. Consequently, we obtain explicit formulas for all the frequencies in the cross-correlation distribution.
tldr: This paper determines the distribution of cross-correlation values for a specific Niho-type decimation over finite fields.
motivation: The cross-correlation problem is fundamental in sequence design, with applications in communications and cryptography.
method: The authors reduce the problem to counting certain subsets, normalize by their product, and evaluate associated character and Kloosterman sums.
result: Explicit formulas for all frequencies in the cross-correlation distribution are obtained.
conclusion: The work provides a complete solution to the cross-correlation distribution for this Niho-type decimation, contributing to classical sequence theory.

title: Near-Field Physical-Layer Authentication Under Impersonation Attacks
authors: Hajar El Hassani, Linda Senigagliesi, Arsenia Chorti
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04879v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper studies physical-layer authentication (PLA) in the near-field regime under impersonation attacks. Unlike the far-field case, where the steering vector depends only on the angle of arrival (AoA), in the near field it depends on both angle and distance. We analyze the attack by minimizing the mean-square error (MSE) between the signal received from a legitimate transmitter Alice and the signal generated by an active attacker Eve. For a single-antenna Eve, we derive the optimal scalar precoder and show that, under the standard second-order Fresnel approximation, perfect impersonation is possible only if Eve has the same angle and the same distance from Bob as Alice. We then extend the analysis to a multi-antenna Eve and derive the optimal precoding vector. In this case, perfect impersonation is possible only if Alice steering vector belongs to the subspace spanned by Eve steering vectors. Simulation results show that, in the near field, a distance difference is sufficient to prevent a successful impersonation attack even when Alice and Eve have the same AoA, and confirm the analytical results.
tldr: The paper analyzes near-field physical-layer authentication under impersonation attacks, showing that a distance difference can prevent successful impersonation even when the attacker shares the same angle of arrival.
motivation: Physical-layer authentication is crucial for securing wireless communications, but near-field effects have been largely ignored; the authors extend the analysis to the near-field regime where steering vectors depend on both angle and distance.
method: The authors formulate the attack as minimizing the mean-square error between the legitimate signal and the attacker's generated signal, deriving optimal precoders for single-antenna and multi-antenna Eve.
result: Perfect impersonation is only possible under specific geometric conditions; simulations confirm that a distance difference suffices to thwart attacks even with same AoA.
conclusion: The near-field regime offers additional security benefits, as distance becomes a parameter that can be exploited to authenticate.

title: Construction Of Finite Hilbert--P\'olya Matrices From Weil's Explicit Formula
authors: Yaoming Shi
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04908v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Starting from the Riemann--[MATH] specialization of Weil's explicit formula, we construct finite real-symmetric Prime--Weil matrices [MATH] from pole, archimedean, and finite prime-power data. This construction is a finite-dimensional arithmetic model within the Hilbert--P\'olya program, which seeks a self-adjoint spectral realization of the nontrivial zeta-zero parameters. Their off-diagonal entries form a Loewner-type divided-difference matrix with a rank-two displacement identity. We formulate the spectral quotient as a Hermitian definite generalized eigenproblem on the fixed zero-mean contrast space. This realization is invariant under positive affine rescaling, avoids ground-vector normalization and an ill-conditioned oblique projector, and preserves the finite quotient spectrum. For a dimension-matched zero-side matrix built from [MATH] distinct positive ordinates [MATH], rational interpolation gives the exact contrast-pencil spectrum [MATH] and positive-parity square spectrum [MATH]. Since the ordinates are inputs, this is a reconstruction theorem. Assuming RH, the same interpolation vector proves [MATH]. At [MATH], Lemke's ground-state quotient and the contrast pencil agree numerically and reproduce the first three zeta ordinates to the reported precision. The remaining problem is a relative prime-to-zero perturbation theorem with uniform control of the compressed metric. No proof of RH is claimed.
tldr: Constructs finite Hilbert-Pólya matrices from Weil's explicit formula to model zeta zeros as eigenvalues of a self-adjoint operator.
motivation: To provide a finite-dimensional spectral realization for the nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function within the Hilbert-Pólya program.
method: From pole, archimedean, and finite prime-power data, constructs real-symmetric Prime-Weil matrices with off-diagonal entries forming a divided-difference matrix, then formulates a Hermitian definite generalized eigenproblem.
result: Shows that for properly chosen zero-side matrices, rational interpolation gives exact spectra, and under RH reproduces the first three zeta ordinates.
conclusion: The remaining challenge is a perturbation theorem; no proof of RH is claimed.

title: Minimum Schubert Codewords And Second-Minimum Grassmann Codewords
authors: Prasant Singh Muskan Khaneja
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04916v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we give a classification of the minimum weight codewords of Schubert codes [MATH] by settling the conjecture proposed by Ghorpade and Singh in 2018, for all values of [MATH] and all [MATH]. We use this classification to prove that a codeword of the Grassmann code [MATH] has the second minimum weight if and only if it is indexed by an element of [MATH] that can be written as the product of a decomposable [MATH]-vector and an alternating [MATH]-vector of rank [MATH]. Finally, we give an enumeration of the second minimum weight codewords of the Grassmann code.
tldr: This paper classifies minimum weight codewords of Schubert codes and characterizes second-minimum weight codewords of Grassmann codes.
motivation: To settle a conjecture by Ghorpade and Singh (2018) and provide explicit characterizations of certain codewords in algebraic codes.
method: The authors use combinatorial and algebraic methods to classify codewords and prove characterizations.
result: They provide a complete classification and enumeration of second-minimum weight codewords of Grassmann codes.
conclusion: The conjecture is resolved, and new insights into the structure of Schubert and Grassmann codes are given.

title: Bipolar Fuzzy Minimum-Weight Satisfiability Under Continuous t-Norms: A Clause-Witness Branch-and-Bound Framework
authors: Mohammad Sedigh Chopannavaz Amin Ghodousian
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04927v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Minimum-weight satisfiability asks for a satisfying Boolean assignment of minimum cost, while many fuzzy decision and knowledge systems operate with graded positive and negative relations rather than crisp literals. This paper introduces a bipolar fuzzy minimum-weight satisfiability problem in which positive and negative clause--variable relations, target clause levels, and variable states are represented in the unit interval. The clause requirements are expressed by bipolar fuzzy relational equalities defined with an arbitrary continuous t-norm. Classical minimum-weight CNF satisfiability is recovered as a crisp special case, independently of the selected t-norm, and an optimal Boolean solution is shown to exist in that specialization even though the proposed formulation uses continuous variables. For the graded problem, clause satisfaction is characterized through admissible variable domains and effective clause-witness sets. This structure leads to an exact clause-witness branch-and-bound method with preprocessing, propagation, lower-point closure, and a disjoint-witness packing bound. Computational experiments verify the solver against explicit witness enumeration, mixed-integer baselines, and external SATLIB formulas; on a focused graded ablation set, the packing bound reduces the median number of explored nodes by about 45 percent relative to the single-row witness bound.
tldr: This paper introduces a novel bipolar fuzzy extension of the minimum-weight satisfiability problem and an exact branch-and-bound algorithm exploiting clause-witness structures.
motivation: Many fuzzy decision and knowledge systems require handling graded positive and negative relations, which are not captured by classical Boolean satisfiability, motivating a generalization to bipolar fuzzy logic.
method: The problem is formalized via bipolar fuzzy relational equalities with continuous t-norms, and exact solving is achieved with a clause-witness branch-and-bound framework incorporating preprocessing, propagation, lower-point closure, and a disjoint-witness packing bound.
result: The proposed solver is validated against explicit enumeration, mixed-integer baselines, and SATLIB instances, showing that the packing bound reduces median explored nodes by about 45% on graded instances.
conclusion: The paper provides a principled formalization and an efficient exact method for bipolar fuzzy minimum-weight satisfiability, advancing fuzzy optimization.

title: Frequency-explicit Convergence Analysis Of A Multiscale Finite Element Method For Highly Heterogeneous Scattering Problems
authors: Z. Kassali T. Chaumont-Frelet
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04930v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We analyze the numerical approximation of time-harmonic scattering by highly heterogeneous penetrable obstacles. These problems are especially challenging in the high-frequency regime, where the size of the scatterer [MATH] is much larger than the wavelength, i.e., the wavenumber [MATH] is such that [MATH]. Here, we further consider the situation where the scatterer contains different materials, with a characteristic size [MATH] such that [MATH]. We propose a high-order multiscale finite element method, and provide an error analysis that is explicit in both [MATH] and [MATH]. Crucially, our error estimates suggest that using a high-order method should reduce the computational cost for large frequencies, which is corroborated by numerical examples.
tldr: This paper presents a multiscale finite element method with explicit error analysis for high-frequency scattering in heterogeneous media.
motivation: The authors address challenges in simulating time-harmonic wave scattering when the scatterer is large and contains small-scale heterogeneities, aiming for accurate and efficient high-frequency solutions.
method: They propose a high-order multiscale finite element method and derive error estimates that are explicit in both the wavenumber and the characteristic size of the heterogeneities.
result: The error analysis indicates that higher-order methods reduce computational cost for large frequencies, corroborated by numerical examples.
conclusion: The multiscale FEM with high-order elements is effective for highly heterogeneous scattering problems, offering performance gains in the high-frequency regime.

title: Testing Equality Of Distributions Via Repeatedly Integrated Quantile Metrics Under Weak Moment Conditions
authors: Zhenfeng Zou, Meng Guan, Panxu Yuan
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04935v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Testing whether two independent samples arise from the same underlying distribution is a fundamental statistical problem. We propose a new class of two-sample distribution tests based on a family of probability metrics [MATH], constructed from repeatedly integrated quantile functions. On their respective domains, these metrics are proved to be genuine distributional distances. The case [MATH] recovers the [MATH]-Wasserstein distance, which requires finite [MATH]-th moments; for [MATH], the proposed metrics are well defined and require only finite first moments. The asymptotic properties of the plug-in statistic are established, including strong consistency and limiting distributions under the null and fixed alternatives. A permutation calibration for finite-sample inference is also proposed. We further derive an asymptotic power function under local alternatives. Finally, the finite-sample performance of the proposed tests is examined through simulation studies, and their reduced sensitivity to extreme upper-tail observations is illustrated through a real data application.
tldr: Introduces a new class of two-sample distribution tests based on repeatedly integrated quantile metrics that require only finite first moments.
motivation: Testing equality of distributions is a fundamental statistical problem, and existing metrics may require higher moments or be overly sensitive to tail behavior.
method: Proposes probability metrics from repeatedly integrated quantile functions, proves they are genuine distances, and establishes asymptotic properties including strong consistency and limiting distributions, with a permutation calibration for finite samples.
result: Demonstrates through theory and simulations that the tests have good finite-sample performance and reduced sensitivity to extreme upper-tail observations.
conclusion: Provides a robust and practical tool for two-sample testing that is less dependent on moment conditions.

title: Quantitative Linear Approximation For Controllability Of Quasi-linear Parabolic Equations
authors: Manish Kumar, Xu Liu, Xu Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04969v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper studies the relationship between the controllability of a quasi-linear parabolic equation and that of its linear counterpart. Under suitable assumptions, we prove that for sufficiently small initial data both systems are null controllable, and that the differences between their corresponding controls and states satisfy a higher-order error estimate. Unlike standard controllability problems, the controls constructed here not only steer the system to a prescribed target at a given terminal time, but are also designed to ensure that the deviation between the nonlinear and linear dynamics obeys the aforementioned estimate. This method is applicable to general nonlinear partial differential equations, and the approximation order for controllability is optimal.
tldr: This paper establishes a quantitative linear approximation result for controllability of quasi-linear parabolic equations, showing that for small initial data, the nonlinear and linear systems are both null controllable with higher-order error estimates between their controls and states.
motivation: To understand how controllability of nonlinear PDEs relates to their linear counterparts, and to construct controls that also ensure small deviation between nonlinear and linear dynamics.
method: Under suitable assumptions, the authors prove null controllability for sufficiently small initial data and derive higher-order error estimates for the differences in controls and states. The approach is applicable to general nonlinear partial differential equations.
result: The method achieves optimal approximation order for controllability, meaning the deviation between nonlinear and linear dynamics satisfies the derived higher-order bound.
conclusion: The work provides a general framework for approximating controllability of nonlinear systems by linear ones with rigorous error guarantees, which is significant for control theory of PDEs.

title: Faster Learning Under Relaxed Local Differential Privacy
authors: Cristina Butucea, Huiyun Tang, Marie-Luce Taupin
abstract: ArXiv:2609.05034v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider density estimation under the relaxed local differential privacy condition that the privatized distributions are [MATH]-close in total variation distance. We show that adding independent noise with a convenient symmetrized Gamma distribution to each sensitive observation attains the [MATH]-TV-LDP. We prove that the deconvolution estimator of [MATH]-Sobolev smooth functions attains the pointwise rate [MATH] up to log factors which is faster than [MATH] under the classical [MATH]-LDP and closer to the nonprivate minimax rate [MATH]. Next, we use a Goldenshluger-Lepski procedure to build a free of the smoothness adaptive procedure and show optimality of our rates in the convolution model of our privatisation scheme. We illustrate the benefits of this simple privacy mechanism by implementing a neural network estimator which does not need to add more noise in the optimization steps. Numerical results show significant improvement of the estimation rate over the Laplace and the private-SGD mechanisms.
tldr: The paper proposes a relaxed local differential privacy (LDP) mechanism using symmetrized Gamma noise to achieve faster density estimation rates than classical LDP.
