motivation: To improve statistical efficiency under local differential privacy by relaxing the privacy condition to total variation distance, enabling faster convergence rates for density estimation.
method: It introduces a privatization scheme adding symmetrized Gamma noise to achieve TV-LDP, then applies deconvolution estimators and an adaptive Goldenshluger-Lepski procedure to attain optimal rates.
result: The proposed estimator achieves pointwise rates faster than classical LDP and close to nonprivate minimax rates, with numerical results showing significant improvement over Laplace and private-SGD mechanisms.
conclusion: Relaxing LDP to a total variation condition allows for more efficient statistical estimation while still providing a privacy guarantee.

title: Reconciling Universal And Uniform Learning With $Q$-Aggregation
authors: Mikael M{\o}ller H{\o}gsgaard, Patrick Rebeschini, Tobias Wegel
abstract: ArXiv:2609.05041v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study regression under bounded responses in terms of excess mean squared error. When the comparator class is finite, this setting is known as model selection aggregation, and achieving minimax excess risk requires improper learning algorithms. Contrary to this, in the universal learning framework no improperness is needed, as simple empirical risk minimization achieves the best-possible exponential learning rate. Hence, the two frameworks suggest different optimal algorithmic principles. This poses the question of best-of-both-worlds guarantees: Are minimax and universal exponential rates achievable by the same algorithm? For finite hypothesis classes, we answer this question in the affirmative by showing that the [MATH]-aggregation estimator - which is known to achieve minimax optimal tails - achieves exponential universal rates. A wide range of other estimators and algorithmic principles (ERM, sequential averaging, pruning, and star estimation) do not achieve both. For countably infinite hypothesis classes, we answer the question in the negative by showing that there is an inherent trade-off between achieving exponential universal and minimax uniform rates. This trade-off is exactly traced by combining optimal algorithms from each world using [MATH]-aggregation. Besides these results, we prove several additional structural results about universal rates in learning with squared loss.
tldr: This paper reconciles minimax and universal learning rates in regression by showing Q-aggregation achieves both for finite classes, but demonstrates a trade-off for countably infinite classes.
motivation: The two learning frameworks (model selection aggregation and universal learning) suggest different optimal algorithmic principles, and it is unclear if a single algorithm can achieve both minimax and universal exponential rates.
method: The authors analyze regression with bounded responses, focusing on the Q-aggregation estimator and comparing it with ERM, sequential averaging, pruning, and star estimation in both finite and countably infinite hypothesis class settings.
result: For finite hypothesis classes, Q-aggregation achieves both minimax optimal tails and exponential universal rates, while other algorithms do not; for countably infinite classes, an inherent trade-off exists, precisely traced by combining optimal algorithms via Q-aggregation.
conclusion: Minimax and universal exponential rates can be simultaneously achieved for finite classes using Q-aggregation, but not for infinite classes, revealing a fundamental trade-off in learning theory.

title: Convex Order And Preservation Of Convexity For Bayesian Posterior Updates
authors: Yuqiong Wang Erhan Bayraktar
abstract: ArXiv:2609.05065v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study how the response of a Bayesian posterior statistic to future observations changes as information accumulates. For a non-decreasing function [MATH], define [MATH], where [MATH] has an arbitrary prior and the observations come from a one-parameter exponential family. Conditioning on the same current value of [MATH], we show that the posterior statistic after additional observations is larger in convex order when the current posterior is based on fewer observations. We also prove preservation of convexity: the expected value of a convex function of the future posterior statistic is convex in the current posterior statistic. Together, these two properties provide structural tools for establishing time-monotonicity results in dynamic Bayesian decision and optimal stopping problems. If the exponential family contains an infinitely divisible distribution, the results extend to a continuous-time observation model through a family of L\'evy processes.
tldr: This paper studies convex ordering properties of Bayesian posterior statistics under exponential family observations, showing that posterior statistics based on fewer observations are larger in convex order and that convexity is preserved, with extensions to continuous-time Lévy models.
motivation: To understand how posterior statistics evolve as more information accumulates, which is crucial for dynamic Bayesian decision problems and optimal stopping.
method: The authors prove that, conditioning on the same current posterior statistic, the posterior statistic after additional observations is larger in convex order when the current posterior is based on fewer observations. They also establish preservation of convexity and extend results to continuous-time settings via Lévy processes.
result: The two properties (convex order monotonicity and preservation of convexity) are rigorously proven, and the results are extended to continuous-time observation models.
conclusion: The findings provide structural tools for establishing time-monotonicity results in dynamic Bayesian decision and optimal stopping problems, though the work is purely classical and disconnected from quantum information science.

title: Simultaneous Change-Point Inference For High-Dimensional Functional Time Series
authors: Colin Decker Axel B\"ucher
abstract: ArXiv:2609.05077v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a framework for simultaneous change-point inference of high-dimensional functional time series. The observations are modeled as temporally dependent vectors whose coordinates take values in possibly different separable Hilbert spaces, thereby covering a broad class of functional data. Heterogeneous mean changes may occur at coordinate-specific locations, and the contemporaneous dependence across coordinates is left unrestricted. Our procedure is based on coordinatewise cumulative-sum statistics and a residual block multiplier bootstrap that provides a common critical value for the global test and all coordinatewise decisions. We establish a nonasymptotic Gaussian approximation, quantitative nonasymptotic bounds for strong family-wise error control under arbitrary mixtures of changed and unchanged coordinates, covariance-adaptive detection guarantees, and simultaneous high-probability bounds for change-point localization. The bounds accommodate high-dimensional regimes in which the number of functional coordinates grows exponentially in a power of the sample size. We investigate finite-sample performance in simulations and illustrate the method using river discharge curves and high-frequency financial log returns.
tldr: This paper develops a framework for simultaneous change-point inference in high-dimensional functional time series using cumulative sum statistics and a block multiplier bootstrap, but it is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, or quantum networks.
motivation: The need for detecting multiple heterogeneous mean changes in functional time series with high-dimensional coordinates and unrestricted cross-sectional dependence.
method: Coordinatewise cumulative-sum statistics combined with a residual block multiplier bootstrap to derive common critical values, along with nonasymptotic Gaussian approximation for inference.
result: Established strong family-wise error control, covariance-adaptive detection guarantees, and simultaneous localization bounds, even when the number of coordinates grows exponentially with sample size.
conclusion: The proposed method effectively handles change-point inference in complex high-dimensional functional time series, as demonstrated via simulations and applications to financial and hydrological data.

title: Blockchain-Enabled Secure Logging For Fiscal Electronic Mechanisms: Evaluation Of The Greek eSEND And myDATA Tax Systems
authors: Panagiotis Mavridis, Anargyros Baklezos, Christos Nikolopoulos
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04356v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper analyzes the implementation of blockchain-based integrity mechanisms in Greek Fiscal Electronic Mechanisms (FEMs) and the central tax information system eSEND. The study examines the cryptographic architecture of fiscal devices, including Electronic Cash Registers, Fiscal Printers, Fiscal Signing Machines, and FEMAS devices, which implement double or triple hash-chain structures to ensure transaction immutability. The transmission protocol between fiscal devices and the central database is also evaluated with respect to encryption, sequential validation, and blockchain verification. In contrast, the architecture of Electronic Invoicing Provider Services and the myDATA central platform is analyzed, highlighting the absence of blockchain-based integrity guarantees. The comparison demonstrates that hardware-based fiscal mechanisms provide stronger guarantees for transaction completeness and tamper resistance than purely software-based invoicing infrastructures. The findings highlight architectural weaknesses in the current e-invoicing framework and propose improvements for ensuring transaction integrity in digital tax ecosystems.
tldr: This paper evaluates blockchain-based integrity mechanisms in Greek fiscal electronic systems, comparing hardware-based fiscal devices with software-based e-invoicing platforms.
motivation: To assess the security and tamper resistance of blockchain implementations in tax systems, particularly in the Greek eSEND and myDATA contexts.
method: Analyzes the cryptographic architecture of fiscal devices, including hash-chain structures and encryption, and compares them with the myDATA platform.
result: Finds that hardware-based fiscal mechanisms provide stronger integrity guarantees than software-based e-invoicing infrastructures.
conclusion: Suggests improvements for the current e-invoicing framework to enhance transaction integrity in digital tax ecosystems.

title: Privacy Failure In Split-LLM Training, The Returned Gradient Nullifies The Decoys
authors: Evangelos Pappas Georgios Politis
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04382v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a systems-security case study of a two-node split-LLM training system whose privacy evaluation passed while leaving an observable channel untested. The Trusted Local Node (TLN) sends protected activations to the Untrusted Cloud Node (UCN), the UCN returns its output, and TLN, holding the private loss, returns the output gradient. The frame the UCN receives mixes real rows with decoys, and the loss ignores the decoys. Their gradients are exactly zero, so the pattern of zeros reveals which rows were real. We measure it with a protocol fixed in advance: a leak injected at known strength to prove the instrument can see one, a shuffled-label control to prove it does not report absent leaks, and a threshold set before the runs. Across nine seeds, the zeros identified the real rows on every frame, 4,096 of 4,096 per run. An attack on the frame contents recovered about one extra token per hundred over a constant-guess baseline (+0.65 to +1.50 percentage points); the shuffled controls recovered nothing. A second set of runs repeated this on a configuration that keeps model quality within budget, so the finding is not confined to a setting nobody would deploy. On both datasets, every such run passed the forward-channel privacy check and the quality check, yet failed that same check once the returned gradient was included. Clipping and noising each row of the gradient closed the leak for about 0.01 nats of held-out cross-entropy. The system is not thereby safe: five classes of attack, including those accumulating observations across training steps, were never measured.
tldr: This paper studies privacy leakage in split-LLM training, showing that returned gradients reveal real data rows despite decoys.
motivation: Privacy evaluations of split-LLM systems may overlook observable channels, such as the pattern of zeros in gradients when decoys are used.
method: The authors conduct a systems-security case study with a fixed protocol: injected leaks, shuffled-label controls, and thresholds, across multiple seeds and datasets.
result: Zero patterns in returned gradients identify real rows on every frame (4096/4096 per run), but gradient clipping and noising close the leak with minimal quality loss.
conclusion: The system remains unsafe as several attack classes are untested; privacy checks must include returned gradients.

title: A Numerical Approach To The Realizability Problems For Memoryless Nash And Epsilon Equilibria In Concurrent Multiplayer Reachability Games
authors: Senthil Rajasekaran, Jean-Fran\c{c}ois Raskin, Moshe Y. Vardi
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04396v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The existence of equilibria, which is called the realizability problem in the formal methods community, for probabilistic undiscounted state-based systems has proven to be an incredibly challenging research setting. In this paper, we consider a restricted version of the classic realizability problem by focusing on equilibria that are both memoryless and numerically constrained. While the restriction to memoryless strategies is relatively common in the literature, numerical constraints, to the best of our knowledge, represent a new and powerful approach. First, we consider the existence of memoryless equilibria when all numbers involved must be rational numbers of a pre-defined limited size. Then, we extend this analysis to field extensions of the rational numbers created through radical algebraic generators. When the basis is provided for the latter, both realizability problems are NP-complete for both exact and epsilon Nash equilibria. Finally, we consider an unconstrained numerical setting. While the characterization of the exact Nash equilibria realizability problem as ETR-complete is one of the most celebrated results in the literature, we demonstrate that the constructions underlying this result are flawed as presented. We then mend said constructions to preserve the ETR upper bound, and note that the lower bound in the literature does not apply to the epsilon-equilibrium setting. Overall, this paper demonstrates an interesting relationship between the complexity of the realizability problem and the "complexity" of the numbers involved in the representations of strategies.
tldr: This paper analyzes the computational complexity of finding memoryless Nash equilibria in concurrent multiplayer reachability games under numerical constraints, yielding NP-complete and ETR-complete results.
motivation: The existence of equilibria is a classic problem in formal verification and multi-agent systems; the authors investigate how limiting the numerical complexity of strategies affects the complexity of this realizability problem.
method: They formalize memoryless equilibria with rational numbers of bounded size and field extensions from radical generators, and refine existing constructions for unconstrained numeric settings.
result: They prove both realizability problems (exact and epsilon) are NP-complete for bounded rationals and algebraic extensions, and correct the faulty ETR upper bound proof while noting the lower bound does not apply to epsilon equilibria.
conclusion: The computational complexity of reaching an equilibrium is closely linked to the numerical representation of the strategies, demonstrating a clear trade-off between expressiveness and tractability.

title: Engineered Persuasion: Evaluating Personalized Pretexts In LLM-Generated Spear Phishing
authors: Jerson Francia, Derek Hansen, Benjamin Schooley, Shydra Valynn Murray
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04410v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models can insert workplace details into phishing pretexts at low cost, but those details may either support or undermine a message's credibility. We recruited 180 U.S. working adults to evaluate simulated, AI-generated phishing emails in a disclosed survey. The emails used four cumulative levels of information: workplace (Level 1); recipient name and job title; job responsibilities; and coworker/shared-project context (Level 4). Participants rated each message's convincingness from 0 to 100, chose one stated action (open the link, investigate, delete, or report), and explained why their highest- and lowest-rated messages stood out. Across 1,436 valid evaluations, convincingness increased by 2.40 points per personalization level in a sensitivity analysis, while the odds of expressing click intention increased by 28\% per level. Among participants who did not express an intention to click, investigation remained common, reporting declined, and deletion increased. A post-hoc descriptive analysis found higher ratings and click intention for messages from a named person who referenced a supplied coworker than for messages from a department or entity. Qualitative coding showed why added detail could help or hurt: details that matched participants' roles and routines supported credibility, while incorrect, vague, or channel-inappropriate details raised suspicion. Together, the results highlight that personalization is not simply a matter of adding more details: it depends on whether the pretext fits the recipient's work context. We discuss how this distinction can inform workplace cybersecurity training.
tldr: This paper evaluates the effectiveness of LLM-generated personalized phishing emails, finding that contextual relevance, not just personalization level, drives credibility and click intentions.
motivation: To understand how LLMs can exploit workplace details in phishing attacks and to inform cybersecurity training.
method: Recruited 180 US working adults to rate simulated AI-generated phishing emails with four levels of personalization (0 to 4), measuring convincingness, click intention, and qualitative feedback.
result: Convincingness increased by 2.40 points per personalization level; click intention odds increased by 28% per level. Details that mismatched roles or context reduced credibility.
conclusion: Personalization effectiveness depends on fit with the recipient's context, suggesting targeted training rather than a simple model of adding details.

title: Nebulon Enterprise Simulated Threats For Phishing Research (NEST-Phish): A Synthetic Enterprise Phishing Email Dataset For Behavioral And Machine-Learning Research
authors: Emily J. Winokur, Lauren S. Treiman, Allen G. Moore, Paul Schutte, Joe Ingram, Danielle N. Sanchez
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04474v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Phishing remains one of the most persistent cyber threats, yet publicly shareable datasets for studying phishing in realistic enterprise email settings remain limited. To address this gap, we introduce a synthetic enterprise phishing email dataset built around a fictitious organization, Nebulon. The dataset spans a broad set of workplace communication themes and includes matched synthetic legitimate and phishing emails with interpretable phishing-cue annotations. Here, ``legitimate'' denotes the non-phishing class, not legitimately occurring organizational emails. Human-subject categorizations and classifier evaluations show that the dataset supports meaningful variation in phishing judgments while also providing learnable signal for supervised detection. This publicly released resource is intended to support future work on phishing detection, human susceptibility, explainability, and benchmark development in enterprise-like contexts.
tldr: Introduces a synthetic enterprise phishing email dataset for behavioral and machine-learning research.
motivation: There is a lack of publicly shareable datasets for phishing research in realistic enterprise email contexts.
method: A synthetic dataset was constructed based on a fictitious organization, featuring matched legitimate and phishing emails with interpretable phishing-cue annotations.
result: Human-subject evaluations and classifier tests confirm the dataset captures meaningful variation and provides learnable signals for detection.
conclusion: This public resource aims to support future work on phishing detection, human susceptibility, explainability, and benchmark development.

title: Client-Side Probing Of Deleted Ridge Statistics In Federated Unlearning
authors: Giovanni Montana Yijun Quan
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04475v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Federated unlearning aims to remove a client's data from a shared model without retraining from scratch. Some efficient systems make deletion exact by storing compact, additive summaries of the training features and broadcasting an updated linear classifier after every accepted change. We show that these broadcasts can also reveal the hidden summaries. A malicious client can submit known changes, use the returned classifiers to identify the server state, and compare states immediately before and after an isolated deletion. This exposes the deleted sample, class, or client summary and can enable its reinsertion. We characterize exactly when the observations contain enough independent information, give a matching optimal construction for unrestricted probes, and derive a more realistic estimator based on additions formed from the attacker's own data. On MNIST and CIFAR-10, high-precision broadcasts permit exact label recovery for every tested sample deletion with both probe types. Lower-precision broadcasts sharply reduce fine-grained recovery, and insufficiently diverse responses prevent identification altogether. Unrestricted probes are readily detected by their size; most individual attacker-data additions resemble honest batches, although we do not claim that the complete sequence is inconspicuous. The results identify a concrete privacy and integrity risk, its algebraic cause, and practical limits involving broadcast precision, update verification, response rate, and concurrent activity.
tldr: The paper reveals that federated unlearning systems broadcasting updated linear classifiers can be probed by malicious clients to recover deleted data.
motivation: Federated unlearning efficiently removes client data by storing additive summaries and broadcasting classifier updates, but these broadcasts may leak hidden summaries.
method: The authors formally characterize when observations contain enough information, develop optimal unrestricted probes and a realistic estimator using attacker's data, and assess detection risk.
result: On MNIST and CIFAR-10, high-precision broadcasts allow exact label recovery for all tested deletions; lower precision and response diversity reduce or prevent recovery.
conclusion: The study identifies a concrete privacy risk in federated unlearning, explains its algebraic cause, and highlights mitigation factors such as broadcast precision and update verification.

title: The Deterministic Hare Core Is Nonempty For Nine-Seat Approval Elections
authors: Jiarui Fang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04497v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Core stability gives approval-based committee elections a strong form of coalitional proportionality, but deterministic existence is not known for an arbitrary number of seats. We prove that every finite election with nine seats has a deterministic Hare-quota core committee. Starting from an eight-seat committee that is both a global Proportional Approval Voting (PAV) maximizer and core stable, we suppose that all one-candidate extensions are blocked and extract an inclusion-minimal closed response system. Singleton responses are eliminated by exact equality rigidity. For the remaining responses, rational Farkas certificates bound every nonpositive PAV add-marginal drift below by [MATH] and force every successor drift above [MATH]. The uniform response chain is irreducible, so stationarity makes these bounds incompatible. The computer-assisted component comprises an exact pointwise check over 7,356 voter types, 36 one-blocker cells, and a symmetry-complete family of 19 two-blocker motifs. Exact certificate archives and standard-library verifiers support these checks. The theorem settles the nine-seat case but does not decide deterministic core existence for arbitrary committee size.
tldr: Proves that every finite election with nine seats has a deterministic Hare-quota core committee.
motivation: To establish the existence of a core-stable committee under Hare quota for a fixed number of seats, which was unknown for nine seats.
method: Starts from an eight-seat committee that is both a global PAV maximizer and core stable, then analyzes blocking responses using exact equality rigidity and rational Farkas certificates, supported by a computer-assisted check over voter types and blocker motifs.
result: The paper proves deterministically that a Hare-quota core committee always exists for nine-seat approval elections.
conclusion: This settles the nine-seat case but leaves the existence problem open for arbitrary committee sizes.

title: Why Is Shap Not A Reliable Standalone Explanation Framework For Malware Detection?
authors: Seyedreza Mohseni, Edward Raff, Manas Gaur
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04626v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine learning is widely used for malware detection, but its decisions must be explained. An analyst needs to know whether a model has learned genuine malicious behavior or only dataset-specific patterns . SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) is the standard tool for this, backed by formal properties such as local accuracy, missingness, and consistency. We argue that these guarantees are insufficient for reliable malware interpretation. We claim SHAP explains a chosen feature-coalition game, not malware behavior in the data. That game is fixed only after the analyst selects the feature players, the missing feature rule, the background distribution, and the simplified input mapping. In static Portable Executable feature spaces, groups such as byte histograms, byte-entropy, strings, headers, sections, imports, and data-directories are not independent signals but are jointly shaped by file structure, packing, compiler behavior, and family conventions. We prove that this dependence makes conditional SHAP dilute a model's feature credit by a factor of [MATH] across [MATH] redundant features, attributes importance to features the model never uses, and even reverses the sign of an unused feature's attribution when the data distribution changes; interventional SHAP, meanwhile, queries off-manifold coalitions that no real executable would exhibit. Experiments on EMBER-2018, EMBER-2024, and BODMAS with fixed LightGBM and XGBoost detectors confirm these effects. We therefore position SHAP as a limited diagnostic that requires an explicitly stated data distribution and domain validation, not a standalone account of malware behavior.
tldr: This paper argues that SHAP explanations are unreliable for malware detection due to feature dependencies, showing conditional and interventional SHAP each have flaws, and positions SHAP as a limited diagnostic rather than a standalone explanation.
motivation: Analysts need to trust that malware detection models have learned genuine malicious behavior, not dataset-specific patterns, and SHAP is the standard tool but its guarantees (local accuracy, missingness, consistency) are insufficient for this purpose.
method: The authors theoretically demonstrate that conditional SHAP dilutes feature credit across redundant features and can reverse unused feature attributions, while interventional SHAP queries off-manifold coalitions; they validate these claims on EMBER-2018, EMBER-2024, and BODMAS datasets with LightGBM and XGBoost detectors.
result: Experiments confirm that SHAP explanations are not standalone reliable, as attribution errors occur due to feature redundancy and off-manifold sampling, and these effects are prominent in real malware detection data.
conclusion: SHAP should be used only as a diagnostic tool with explicitly stated data distribution and domain validation, not as a standalone account of malware behavior.

title: Memory-Efficient Designs For Word-Wise Universal Fully Homomorphic Encryption
authors: Ardhi Wiratama Baskara Yudha, Erwin Eko Wahyudi, Rian Adam Rajagede, Qian Lou, Yan Solihin
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04769v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) enables computation on encrypted data, preserving privacy throughout analysis. While its privacy is very strong, FHE is much slower to execute than the original computation. In particular, due to the recent success in accelerating its compute, the performance bottleneck shifts to the memory, especially considering that FHE magnifies the data size by orders of magnitude, resulting in a low arithmetic intensity. We propose BXT, an FHE optimization framework that mitigates the memory bottleneck through four techniques: (1) ciphertext compression, which regenerates ciphertext components from seeds during execution; (2) ciphertext serialization, which packs coefficients as bit arrays and unpacks them during L2-to-L1 transfer; (3) delayed seed generation, which defers PRNG-heavy offline work across aggregated operations; and (4) ciphertext digit pruning guided by fault-aware training tailored for Universal FHE. On CNN inference, the BXT-CSO50 configuration effectively achieves up to 3.8[MATH] speedup over the 100x GPU baseline with less than 1% accuracy loss at 50% comparison precision.
tldr: This paper proposes BXT, an optimization framework for Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) that mitigates memory bottlenecks via compression, serialization, delayed seed generation, and digit pruning.
motivation: FHE is slow and memory-intensive due to data size magnification, shifting the performance bottleneck to memory despite recent compute accelerations.
method: BXT employs four techniques: ciphertext compression via seeded regeneration, ciphertext serialization with bit arrays, delayed seed generation for PRNG-heavy offline work, and digit pruning with fault-aware training tailored for Universal FHE.
result: On CNN inference, BXT-CSO50 achieves up to 3.8x speedup over the 100x GPU baseline with less than 1% accuracy loss at 50% comparison precision.
conclusion: The proposed memory-efficient designs effectively alleviate the memory bottleneck in FHE, offering significant performance improvements with minimal accuracy impact.

title: Injected And Leaked: Actively Inducing Side-Channel Leakage Using Electromagnetic Injection And Hardware Nonlinearity
authors: Haoran Yan, Ziyu Shao, Shuhao Zhang, Qinhong Jiang, Yan Long
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04785v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Electromagnetic (EM) side-channel leakage and injection are typically treated as distinct physical phenomena, threatening data confidentiality and integrity respectively. This work investigates how EM injection can be used to amplify side-channel leakage that is otherwise infeasible. We introduce a novel framework for Injection-Induced EM Side Channels to enable integrated, closed-loop EM security analysis. Our theoretical modeling and experimental measurements reveal that nonlinear hardware components, such as ubiquitous amplifiers, analog-to-digital converters, and power converters, can modulate secret electrical signals onto an injected EM carrier and thus upconvert low-frequency secrets into measurable EM emissions. By tuning the injection frequency and amplitude, adversaries gain the ability to actively shape the effective spectrum and entropy of the resulting leakage. We design InjectEave attack and demonstrate eavesdropping on the audio played through wired and wireless headphones from up to 30 m away with accessible RF equipment, as well as in through-wall scenarios, and characterize injection-induced EM leakage of other low-frequency secrets such as power consumption of smart home devices and analog sensor inputs. Case studies further demonstrate how the proposed techniques enable closed-loop eavesdropping and manipulation of landline-phone conversations. Finally, we analyze the broader security challenges and mitigations.
tldr: The paper introduces a framework for injection-induced EM side channels, using electromagnetic injection to amplify otherwise infeasible side-channel leakage for eavesdropping attacks.
motivation: EM side-channel leakage and injection are typically separate threats; this work aims to unify them to achieve active amplification of weak signals, enabling long-range eavesdropping.
method: The authors model the nonlinearity of hardware components, then use EM injection to upconvert low-frequency secrets onto a carrier, and design the InjectEave attack to measure and decode the resulting emissions.
result: They demonstrate eavesdropping on audio from wired and wireless headphones up to 30 m away, through walls, and characterize leakage from power consumption and sensor inputs, as well as manipulating landline phone conversations.
conclusion: The work reveals a new class of side-channel threats and discusses mitigations, but it is entirely unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, or quantum networks.

title: ReCAST: Restoration-aware Cascaded Stage-wise Training For Obfuscated Sms Risk Classification
authors: Jieyun Huang, Yi Shen, Kaikai Zhao, Jiangze Yan, Wenjing Zhang, Ping Chen, Ning Wang, Zhaoxiang Liu, Kai Wang, Shiguo Lian
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04878v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fraudulent messages sent via Short Message Service (SMS) are increasingly obfuscated to evade cost-conscious classifiers in production systems. In Chinese SMS, attackers can exploit a wide range of carefully crafted obfuscation strategies to hide risk-bearing phrases while preserving human readability, making direct classification brittle under real-world latency and throughput constraints. We propose ReCAST, a Restoration-aware Cascaded Stage-wise Training framework for robust obfuscated Chinese SMS classification. ReCAST distills a large teacher model's de-obfuscation ability into a smaller deployable student model by supervising obfuscated span detection, obfuscation type prediction, and text restoration, and then uses the restoration-aware student for downstream risk classification. Experiments on an internally constructed real-world Chinese SMS benchmark show that ReCAST substantially improves classification performance over directly trained baselines under obfuscation. The results suggest that restoration-aware distillation offers a practical path toward robust SMS risk classification with smaller deployable models under production-oriented constraints.
tldr: Proposes a restoration-aware cascaded training framework to improve robustness of Chinese SMS risk classification against obfuscation.
motivation: Fraudulent SMS increasingly use obfuscation to evade classifiers; production constraints require smaller deployable models that remain robust.
method: Uses teacher-student distillation where the student learns to detect obfuscation spans, predict obfuscation types, and restore the original text before classification.
result: Experiments on a real-world Chinese SMS benchmark show substantial improvement over direct training baselines under obfuscation.
conclusion: Restoration-aware distillation provides a practical way to build robust and compact SMS risk classifiers.

title: TPMSpy: Validation Of Measured Boot Systems By Low-Level Tracing Of Tpm Usage
authors: Petr Svenda Roman Lacko
abstract: ArXiv:2609.05011v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Measured Boot extends trust in a booted system by recording cryptographic measurements of executed software and system state into a Trusted Platform Module (TPM), enabling subsequent verification through remote attestation. Although this mechanism is increasingly deployed in contemporary operating systems, its practical security depends on whether implementations measure the expected components under the expected conditions, yet this is not checked systematically. We propose a platform-agnostic method for analysing low-level TPM usage at the level of virtualized system--TPM interactions. It enables independent reconstruction and validation of the TPM Event Log without relying on the quoting mechanism itself. Because it does not depend on implementation details, it is applicable to both open and closed systems. We demonstrate the method on both Linux and Windows and conduct a systematic longitudinal analysis of Linux systems with systemd versions 245--258 (2020--2025), examining how Measured Boot usage evolved and observing wide divergence. No single usage pattern emerged amongst systems, warranting customized analysis. The analysis identifies undocumented behavioural changes, reveals inconsistent measurements of user-space systemd services, which prevent reliable remote attestation and LUKS disk decryption on such systems.
tldr: This paper presents a platform-agnostic method to validate Measured Boot implementations by low-level tracing of TPM usage, without relying on the quoting mechanism.
motivation: The security of Measured Boot depends on whether implementations measure expected components under expected conditions, yet this is not checked systematically.
method: The authors reconstruct and validate the TPM Event Log by analyzing virtualized system-TPM interactions, making the method independent of implementation details.
result: Demonstrated on Linux and Windows, with a longitudinal study of Linux systemd versions (245-258) revealing divergent usage patterns and undocumented behavioral changes that can break remote attestation and LUKS decryption.
conclusion: The method provides a way to audit Measured Boot systems, but current implementations show inconsistency, motivating customized analysis.

title: Beyond Maintenance Manual Multimodal Rag: Suggesting What Tool
authors: Md Rashedul Islam Seongjun Ha
abstract: ArXiv:2609.05116v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Aircraft technicians are required to consult the maintenance manual (MM) for nearly every task, and locating the relevant procedure across hundreds of pages remains time-consuming. Multimodal retrieval augmented generation (MRAG) has been proposed to address this, allowing technicians to retrieve procedures, together with the accompanying figures, through natural-language queries. However, retrieval alone does not tell the technicians which tools the task requires. The MM identifies special tools only when the corresponding step is reached, and it does not state hand tool requirements at all; to select hand tools, technicians are required to find the hardware dimension from the illustrated parts catalog (IPC) and infer the right tool from it. We therefore propose MRAG-SWAT, an extension of the MRAG pipeline that returns the required hand tools and special tools alongside the retrieved procedure. The framework was implemented for the Lycoming IO-360-N1A engine and demonstrated on eight test queries. By presenting the correct tools together with the procedure, MRAG-SWAT may help reduce repeated trips to the tool crib, prevent damage to aircraft caused by improper tool selection, and thereby avoid additional maintenance tasks and support continued airworthiness.
tldr: This paper proposes MRAG-SWAT, an extension of multimodal retrieval augmented generation that suggests required tools for aircraft maintenance tasks alongside retrieved procedures.
motivation: Aircraft technicians need to consult maintenance manuals for procedures but also must determine required tools, which are not always explicitly mentioned. This leads to inefficiency and potential errors.
method: The framework extends the MRAG pipeline by incorporating information from the illustrated parts catalog to infer and return both hand and special tools relevant to the retrieved procedure.
result: The framework was implemented for a specific engine and demonstrated on eight test queries, showing that the correct tools can be presented together with the procedure.
conclusion: Presenting correct tools alongside procedures may reduce repeated trips to the tool crib and prevent damage from improper tool selection, thereby supporting continued airworthiness.

title: Tier: Threat Implicitness Benchmark For Evaluating Llm Safety Behaviors
authors: Thu-Hien Trinh-Thi, Hai-Yen Vong, Thanh-Ha Ung-Dung, Tram Ho
abstract: ArXiv:2609.05117v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Current LLM safety benchmarks largely rely on binary metrics, overlooking how models respond to harmful prompts with varying threat implicitness. We introduce TIER, a Threat Implicitness Benchmark for behavioral safety evaluation of LLMs. TIER covers four risk domains and four threat levels, from explicit harmful requests to sophisticated jailbreaks. Responses are assessed using a six-label behavior scale and two independent LLM judges. Experiments on six open-weight LLMs show that safety behaviors evolve gradually across threat levels rather than shifting directly from refusal to compliance. Contextual prompts yield the most diverse behaviors, while jailbreaks reveal the largest robustness gaps. Furthermore, models with similar Attack Success Rates can exhibit distinct response distributions, highlighting the need for behavior-aware LLM safety evaluation.
tldr: Introduces TIER, a threat implicitness benchmark for LLM safety behaviors with four risk domains and threat levels, using a six-label behavior scale and LLM judges.
motivation: Current LLM safety benchmarks rely on binary metrics, overlooking how models respond to harmful prompts with varying threat implicitness, necessitating a nuanced behavioral evaluation.
method: TIER covers four risk domains and four threat levels, and responses are assessed using a six-label behavior scale by two independent LLM judges, tested on six open-weight LLMs.
result: Safety behaviors evolve gradually across threat levels, contextual prompts yield the most diverse behaviors, jailbreaks reveal the largest robustness gaps, and models with similar Attack Success Rates can exhibit distinct response distributions.
conclusion: Highlights the need for behavior-aware LLM safety evaluation beyond binary attack success metrics.

title: Understanding The Privacy-Preserving Potential Of Http/2 Against Webpage Fingerprinting
authors: Bogdan Cebere, Prateek Kumar, Sylvain Chatel, Wouter Lueks, Christian Rossow
abstract: ArXiv:2609.05119v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Website fingerprinting (WF) attacks can infer which webpage a user visits from encrypted HTTPS traffic alone, compromising privacy even without decryption. WF defenses commonly shape traffic through noise, padding, delays, or flow splitting, yet they are most often studied from the perspective of encapsulating protocols like Tor or VPN rather than at the application layer (HTTP). In this work, we focus on application-layer defenses enabled by the most widely deployed version of HTTP, HTTP/2. We demonstrate how known defenses can be emulated through HTTP/2 features at the client side (HTTPOS, LLaMA, FRONT, Tamaraw) and the server side (ALPaCA, Tamaraw). We further show that HTTP/2 features, such as proactive resource suggestion, multiplexing, and flow control, offer untapped potential for lightweight yet effective defenses deployable at both endpoints. We evaluate these defenses using a unified blueprint that calibrates defense parameters per dataset, then combines practical attacks, information-theoretic leakage estimates, and overhead measurements. For each defense, this framework identifies the strongest hyperparameter-tuned fingerprinting model and estimates the residual uncertainty induced by the defense using two information-theoretic leakage estimators, all while accounting for the defense's privacy-overhead trade-offs.
tldr: This paper explores HTTP/2 features for website fingerprinting defenses, evaluating their privacy-overhead trade-offs.
motivation: Website fingerprinting attacks can infer a user's visited pages from encrypted traffic, and defenses are often placed at lower protocol layers, neglecting application-layer options like HTTP/2.
method: The authors emulate known defenses via HTTP/2 features and propose new ones, then evaluate all using a unified framework that calibrates parameters, combines practical attacks, information-theoretic leakage estimators, and overhead measurements.
result: The framework identifies the strongest hyperparameter-tuned fingerprinting model and estimates residual uncertainty induced by each defense, accounting for privacy-overhead trade-offs.
conclusion: HTTP/2 features offer untapped potential for lightweight, effective defenses against website fingerprinting, deployable at both client and server sides.

title: Cutting Down The Tower: Single-Exponential Envy-Free Cake Cutting
authors: Yannan Bai Qilin Ye
abstract: ArXiv:2609.05191v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Envy-free cake cutting is a central problem in fair division with a striking divide between existence and computation. Classical topology guarantees that envy-free allocations exist, yet finding one efficiently turned out to be much harder, and this problem has resisted decades of work. A well-known result by Aziz and Mackenzie established the existence of a bounded protocol for every [MATH], but its query bound is [MATH]. A tighter analysis by Sokolov subsequently reduced this upper bound to [MATH], the best known prior to this work. In contrast, the general lower bound, due to Procaccia, is merely [MATH]. We close much of this massive gap with a protocol using at most [MATH] queries. At a high level, our protocol repeatedly allocates some cake without creating envy until the remaining problem involves fewer agents. The main difficulty is to ensure that, when we later put these allocations together, we neither assign any cake twice nor create envy. To overcome this difficulty, we develop a new construction using only polynomially many partial allocations, replacing the [MATH] partial allocations used in previous work. Overall, our protocol gives the first single-exponential query bound for finding a complete envy-free allocation with arbitrary nonatomic, additive valuations.
tldr: This paper proposes a new envy-free cake cutting protocol that achieves a single-exponential query bound, dramatically improving on previous double-exponential results.
motivation: The query complexity of envy-free cake cutting had a massive gap between upper and lower bounds, and the authors aimed to significantly reduce the upper bound.
method: The protocol repeatedly allocates cake to subsets of agents without envy, using only polynomially many partial allocations, and carefully combines them to avoid duplication and envy.
result: They achieved the first single-exponential query bound for envy-free allocation with arbitrary nonatomic additive valuations, closing much of the gap.
conclusion: This work shows that envy-free cake cutting is computationally more tractable than previously thought, though it remains exponential.

title: Governing Bring Your Own Ai: A Parameterized Maturity Model
authors: John Hastings Dare Bello
abstract: ArXiv:2609.05236v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Employees are increasingly using personally owned generative AI tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude for their daily work. This practice is known as Bring Your Own AI (BYOAI), which is a distinct form of Shadow AI in which employee-authenticated personal accounts are used outside of enterprise identity and security controls. Existing frameworks were designed for AI tools managed by organizations, and their coverage does not extend to unmanaged AI tools used with a personal account. In addressing these issues, we developed a governance model through a systematic review of the literature that produces a risk taxonomy and a framework-engagement profile. We also developed a parameterized governance model that measures how much a level of governance maturity reduces residual risk. A five-level maturity ladder is coupled to a technical control architecture through a chain in which the coverage of the control layer influences the security outcomes. Our study of a curated corpus of 30 records (24 research studies and 6 framework documents) indicated that the most prominent categories identified were data exposure and compliance, and framework engagement was inconsistent. Three mutually supporting pillars (technical, governance, and human) were established to support safeguards. Additionally, the results of the model demonstrated that prohibition-based solutions will result in residual risk levels close to those achieved through baseline solutions. Under the specified parameterization, layered control-based solutions substantially reduce modeled exfiltration risk and increase enforceable coverage.
tldr: This paper proposes a governance maturity model for unmanaged employee use of personal generative AI tools (BYOAI), addressing risks like data exposure and compliance gaps.
motivation: Existing AI governance frameworks focus on managed tools, leaving security and compliance gaps for personal-account AI use.
method: A systematic literature review created a risk taxonomy, and a parameterized maturity model linked control layers to residual risk reduction.
result: Data exposure and compliance dominate risks; layered technical controls significantly reduce exfiltration risk compared to prohibition.
conclusion: Effective BYOAI governance requires integrating technical, governance, and human-centric safeguards.

title: Closing Gaps In Online Fair Division
authors: Nicholas Teh Tzeh Yuan Neoh
abstract: ArXiv:2609.05310v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the online fair division of indivisible items, where items arrive one at a time and must be allocated immediately and irrevocably. We address three central open questions in the literature. First, we show that no online algorithm can guarantee any positive multiplicative approximation to proportionality up to any [MATH] goods (PROP[MATH]) against an adaptive adversary. This remains true even when the total number of goods is known in advance, all values lie in [MATH], and every good is positively valued by at most two agents. This impossibility extends to a broad range of standard envy-based, proportionality-based, and share-based notions currently studied in the literature. We also establish the analogous impossibility for chores. Second, in the setting with predictions, a lightweight prediction of the maximum item value was previously known to give [MATH]-PROP1, leaving open whether the dependence on [MATH] is necessary. We give a deterministic [MATH]-PROP1 algorithm against adaptive adversaries. More generally, if the algorithm is given an upper bound [MATH] on the number of agents who value any good positively, the guarantee improves to [MATH] and remains constant under one-sided prediction error. When the total number of goods ([MATH]) is known in advance and [MATH], we further give, for every fixed [MATH], a deterministic algorithm that simultaneously guarantees [MATH]-PROP1 and [MATH] maximum additive envy after normalizing each agent's values by their maximum item value. Third, against a non-adaptive adversary, we determine the tight high-probability PROP1 guarantee of the classical Like rule, which assigns each good uniformly among the agents who value it positively. Unlike uniform random allocation, its guarantee improves when fewer agents value the same good.
tldr: This paper addresses open questions in online fair division of indivisible items, proving impossibility results and designing algorithms for proportional allocation under various adversary models.
motivation: To understand the fundamental limits of online fair division and to provide algorithms with improved guarantees when predictions or knowledge about the number of agents are available.
method: The paper uses theoretical analysis, constructing adversarial scenarios, and designing deterministic algorithms with predictions; it also analyzes the Like rule in high probability.
result: It proves that no online algorithm can guarantee a positive multiplicative approximation to PROP* against adaptive adversaries, even with restricted valuations; provides deterministic algorithms with improved guarantees given predictions; and determines tight high-probability guarantees of the Like rule against non-adaptive adversaries.
conclusion: The findings close several gaps in the understanding of online fair division, offering tight bounds and practical algorithms with minimal prediction requirements.

title: Machine Unlearning As Private Retroactive Algorithms
authors: Haim Kaplan, Refael Kohen, Yishay Mansour, Kobbi Nissim, Uri Stemmer
abstract: ArXiv:2609.05329v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine unlearning typically aims to emulate retraining from scratch: upon a deletion request, the unlearning algorithm should produce an outcome that would have been obtained had the deleted point never been included. Recent work has shown that this emulation requirement carries no meaningful privacy semantics against an adversary who observes a sequence of releases. Machine unlearning is thus not a privacy question per se, but rather a data maintenance question, which is precisely the subject of retroactive algorithms. These are algorithms supporting modifications of past operations, guaranteeing that all subsequent answers reflect the revised history as if it had always been in force. We put forward a definition of private retroactive algorithms, combining the retroactivity requirement with differential privacy under continual observation. We present constructions achieving both privacy and retroactivity at no asymptotic cost over privacy alone for linear statistics, clustering, and histograms, alongside impossibility results.
tldr: This paper introduces private retroactive algorithms for machine unlearning, combining retroactivity with differential privacy to achieve both at no extra asymptotic cost.
motivation: Machine unlearning's standard emulation of retraining does not offer meaningful privacy, so the authors reframe it as a data maintenance problem addressed by retroactive algorithms.
method: They define private retroactive algorithms that support deletion requests while ensuring differential privacy under continual observation, and construct such algorithms for linear statistics, clustering, and histograms.
result: The constructions achieve privacy and retroactivity with no loss in asymptotic efficiency compared to privacy alone, and they also provide impossibility results.
conclusion: This work offers a new framework for machine unlearning that integrates formal privacy guarantees, with efficient mechanisms for specific data structures.

title: Propagation Model For Ssc Attacks: Why Sbom (tools) Don't Tell The Whole Truth
authors: Ljubica Grgic, Lazar Maksimovic, Pavel Laskov
abstract: ArXiv:2609.05380v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ensuring security of software supply chains (SSC) is indispensable in today's world of modern software practices. SBOM (tools) have been introduced as relevant building blocks to ensure the transparency of SSCs. However they have serious limitations in practices as their vulnerability detection and interpretation capacity is not sufficient to explain exploitability effects that can propagte through the whole chain. To address this gap, we propose a propagation-centred approach to SSC security and introduce a four-stage propagation model. We empirically evaluate four open-source SBOM tools against each stage using three projects and Log4j vulnerability as our test case. Our results show that current SBOM tools systematically support only Stage 1 (Structural Exposure) and Stage 2 (Vulnerability Class Presence) while Stage 3 (Code Reachability) and Stage 4 (Taint Path Analysis) require capabilities absent from the SBOM ecosystem. We argue that putting propagation effects at the centre of SSC security research is essential to prevent cyber risk evolving into systemic risks. Our research findings contribute to a future research and design of modern SSC security tools.
tldr: The paper introduces a four-stage propagation model for software supply chain attacks and evaluates SBOM tools, finding they lack capabilities for code reachability and taint analysis.
motivation: SBOM tools have limitations in detecting vulnerability exploitability propagation across software supply chains, posing systemic risks.
method: Proposes a propagation-centered model with four stages (structural exposure, vulnerability class presence, code reachability, taint path analysis) and empirically tests four open-source SBOM tools using three projects and the Log4j vulnerability.
result: SBOM tools systematically support only the first two stages and lack the capabilities required for stages 3 and 4.
conclusion: Supply chain security research should focus on propagation effects to prevent cyber risks from becoming systemic.

title: Hardware-conscious Software Training For Deep Neural Network Inference Accelerator Chips To Recover Accuracy Degradation Due To Hardware Variabilities
authors: Takashi Ohsawa Shuchao Gao
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04259v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Deep neural network (DNN) has been widely applied in various industries. Specialized chips are being discussed for the purpose of achieving lower power consumption with higher throughput. Hardware variations introduced during the process of chip manufacturing are the main reason for affecting the inference accuracies. In this paper, we propose hardware-conscious software training (HCST) method which enables high inference accuracies even under the influence of hardware variations.
tldr: This paper proposes hardware-conscious software training (HCST) to mitigate accuracy degradation in DNN inference due to hardware variability in specialized chips.
motivation: Hardware variations during chip manufacturing can significantly degrade inference accuracy of DNNs on specialized accelerator chips, necessitating a training approach that compensates for these variations.
method: The paper introduces HCST, a training method that aims to make deep neural networks robust to hardware-induced variations, presumably by modeling or incorporating hardware characteristics during training.
result: HCST enables high inference accuracies even under the influence of hardware variations, as claimed in the abstract.
conclusion: The proposed method helps recover accuracy loss caused by hardware variabilities, making DNN inference more reliable on specialized hardware.

title: Abstraction Agent
authors: Longbo Huang Boning Li
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04303v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Information abstraction, which groups strategically similar private states into a tractable number of buckets, is essential for scaling game-solving algorithms to large imperfect-information games. Constructing effective abstractions, however, has traditionally required domain-specific evaluators such as hand-strength calculators or equity estimators, which demand expert knowledge and engineering effort and are unavailable for most less-studied games. We propose the Abstraction Agent, a zero-shot pipeline that uses a large language model (LLM) to discover continuous strategic features from a natural-language game description, score private states on these features, and cluster them into abstraction buckets, without any game-specific evaluator, training data, or game-tree traversal during abstraction construction. The pipeline runs in four phases: feature discovery with calibration anchors, batched private-state scoring, correlation-based feature selection, and [MATH]-means clustering. The resulting abstractions reduce lifted-strategy exploitability by up to 62% relative to an expected-hand-strength baseline on heads-up no-limit Texas hold'em (HUNL) turn endgames, and beat a scalar rank baseline at every granularity on ROVER Trials, an original game absent from any pretraining corpus. Beyond these quantitative benchmarks, the pipeline transfers with unchanged prompts to four-card Pot-Limit Omaha, HUNL preflop and flop, and Riichi Mahjong, where the discovered features track each game's recognized strategic concepts. This is structured knowledge elicitation: converting implicit strategic knowledge in LLM parameters into explicit numerical features for downstream algorithmic computation. The code is available at [URL].
tldr: This paper proposes an LLM-based pipeline to automatically discover strategic features for abstraction in imperfect-information games, reducing exploitability in poker and other games.
motivation: Traditional abstraction construction requires domain-specific evaluators, which are hard to build for less-studied games; the authors aim to automate feature discovery using natural language game descriptions.
method: The Abstraction Agent pipeline uses an LLM to generate strategic features from a game description, score private states on these features, select informative features via correlation, and cluster states into abstraction buckets with k-means.
result: The method reduces exploitability by up to 62% versus a hand-strength baseline in HUNL turn endgames, beats a scalar rank baseline in ROVER Trials, and transfers to PLO, HUNL preflop/flop, and Riichi Mahjong with unchanged prompts.
conclusion: The work demonstrates structured knowledge elicitation from LLMs to produce explicit numerical features for downstream algorithmic computation, enabling zero-shot abstraction for novel games.

title: A Class Of High-order discontinuous-Galerkin Methods Satisfying Infinitely Many Entropy Conditions With Provable Error Estimates And Strong Convergence For General Nonlinear Conservation Laws
authors: Chi-Wang Shu Yuanzhe Wei
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04687v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a novel framework for deriving semi-discrete discontinuous-Galerkin (DG) methods using operator semigroups for scalar conservation laws, then apply it to construct a class of high-order OFDG-type schemes [13] satisfying infinitely many local entropy inequalities with general E-fluxes on non-uniform meshes. Such schemes are further generalized to systems of conservation laws in any number of space dimensions by using entropy stable numerical fluxes in the sense of [1]. Finally, we prove optimal error estimates for smooth solutions to nonlinear scalar conservation laws, and prove strong convergence for discontinuous solutions to strictly convex conservation laws via compensated compactness.
tldr: This paper presents a novel framework for constructing high-order discontinuous-Galerkin methods that satisfy infinitely many entropy conditions for nonlinear conservation laws, with provable error estimates and strong convergence.
motivation: The work aims to develop robust numerical methods for nonlinear conservation laws that respect entropy conditions, which are crucial for accuracy and stability in simulations.
method: The authors use operator semigroups to derive semi-discrete DG schemes and construct OFDG-type flux schemes satisfying local entropy inequalities on non-uniform meshes, extending to systems via entropy stable fluxes.
result: They prove optimal error estimates for smooth solutions and demonstrate strong convergence for discontinuous solutions of strictly convex conservation laws using compensated compactness.
conclusion: This provides a theoretical foundation for high-order DG methods with enhanced entropy stability, which is significant for computational fluid dynamics and related fields.

title: Ultrafast Control Of Lifetime In High Q Anisotropic Plasmon Polaritons
authors: Romain Tirole, Giacomo Venturi, Emroz Khan, Lin Jing, Lin Nan, Nicola Melchioni, Andrea Mancini, Antonio Ambrosio, Andrea Al\`u
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04403v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Losses are a major roadblock in the technological implementation of surface plasmons at optical frequencies. The recent emergence of MoOCl2, a correlated van-der-Waals material with strongly anisotropic optical properties, offers new avenues to circumvent this limit. We report the far-field observation of high-Q surface plasmon polaritons in this material, arising from the anisotropic hybridisation of surface plasmons and dielectric modes. We then explore nonlinear pumping of intraband electrons to the conduction band in these structures, leading, contrary to intuition, to an abrupt increase in the lifetime of the polariton resonance, despite the injection of hot electrons. This counterintuitive phenomenon stems from the competition between photon and plasmon excitations in a lenticular polariton resonance, yielding a largely tuneable lifetime at ultrafast speeds.
tldr: This paper reports ultrafast control of the lifetime of anisotropic plasmon polaritons in MoOCl2, a correlated van-der-Waals material, through nonlinear pumping of intraband electrons.
motivation: Losses hinder the technological implementation of surface plasmons at optical frequencies; the authors explore a novel material and pumping scheme to overcome this.
method: The authors observe high-Q surface plasmon polaritons via far-field spectroscopy and investigate nonlinear pumping of intraband electrons to the conduction band.
result: Counterintuitively, pumping leads to an abrupt increase in the polariton resonance lifetime due to competition between photon and plasmon excitations.
conclusion: The work demonstrates a largely tuneable polariton lifetime at ultrafast speeds, but it is not directly relevant to the user's research interests.

title: Optimal Stratified Allocation For Rare-Event Onset Forecasting In Dependent Sequences
authors: Jaskaran Singh
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04420v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let a finite population of n labelled examples carry a class-weighted loss, with pi*n in a rare positive class weighted by N0/N1. We study estimation of total risk from a subsample K << n under designs allocating K0 and K1 draws to the two strata. We derive the exact finite-population variance of the weighted risk estimator under class-conditional sampling without replacement and solve for the optimal allocation. The class multiplier inflates positive-stratum dispersion by the imbalance ratio, causing that ratio to cancel from the optimal allocation and making equal, rather than proportional, allocation the natural default. Simple random sampling is dominated by an explicit between-stratum term; an exact bias identity shows that cluster-representative selection has no general unbiasedness guarantee; and a Serfling bound transfers the allocation result to selection error over a finite candidate set. Under the implemented truncation, the realised allocation ratio is gamma=min(2*pi/f,1), independent of n, yielding the parameter-free efficiency prediction A(pi,f)=gamma/[pi(1-pi)(1+gamma)^2]. A separate measurability result bounds the record occupied by a labelled example, determining the required train-test separation and controlling departure from block independence under absolute regularity. We test these predictions on forecasting the onset of statistically explosive price regimes, dated ex post by the Phillips-Shi-Yu procedure, using 350 U.S. equities from 2004-2011 with under 1% positive rows and five purged forward blocks. The predicted ordering of the four designs holds, and at the 10-day horizon the five design points are ordered exactly as predicted by A (Spearman rho=1, exact p=0.0167). The predicted dependence on pi across horizons does not hold; we identify the channels lying outside the design-based argument.
tldr: The paper derives optimal stratified sampling allocation for rare-event onset forecasting in dependent sequences, applied to explosive price regimes.
motivation: To estimate total risk from a small subsample when rare positive events exist, and to determine the optimal allocation between strata.
method: The authors derive the exact finite-population variance for class-conditional sampling without replacement, solve for the optimal allocation, and provide bias identities and a Serfling bound.
result: They show that optimal allocation tends to equal rather than proportional, and test predictions on 350 U.S. equities; the design ordering holds at one horizon but not across others.
conclusion: The design-based argument is partially validated; discrepancies across horizons are attributed to factors outside the design framework.

title: Extended Graphon Mean-Field Games In Discrete Time
authors: Hamed Amini, Zhongyuan Cao, G\"ok\c{c}e Dayan{\i}kl{\i}, Mathieu Lauri\`ere, Kexin Shao, Agn\`es Sulem
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04737v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we study games involving a continuum of heterogeneous players in the discrete-time setting with finite state spaces and continuous action spaces. We introduce a new model that incorporates joint state-action interactions within the graphon-weighted aggregate, described by a coupled forward-backward system. We establish the existence of graphon mean-field equilibria and characterize them through this forward-backward system. Additionally, we provide uniqueness results under monotonicity and contraction conditions. To illustrate the practical relevance of our framework, we solve an example of portfolio liquidation with price impact. We provide numerical results for three different graphons and two different initial distributions, illustrating the impact of the network's structure and the distribution heterogeneity on the distribution and the policy.
tldr: This paper introduces a discrete-time graphon mean-field game model with heterogeneous players and joint state-action interactions, establishing equilibrium existence and uniqueness.
motivation: To analyze large-population games with heterogeneous players interacting via a network structure (graphon) in discrete time, exemplified by portfolio liquidation.
method: The model couples forward-backward equations for the aggregate state-action profile, with proof techniques for existence and uniqueness under monotonicity/contraction conditions.
result: They prove existence of graphon mean-field equilibria, derive uniqueness conditions, and provide numerical simulations for portfolio liquidation across different graphons.
conclusion: The discrete-time graphon mean-field framework offers a tractable way to study network effects in heterogeneous-agent games, with practical relevance in finance and beyond.

title: The Security Feature Location Problem
authors: Kevin Hermann, Sven Peldszus, Thorsten Berger, Adam Shostack
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04899v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Software security must be realized through security features such as authentication and encryption, but which features does a system implement, and where? We present security feature location: the task of relating code locations to security features, enabling developers to understand security implementations and assess whether intended security properties are enforced.
tldr: This paper introduces the task of security feature location, which relates code locations to security features such as authentication and encryption.
motivation: Understanding which security features a system implements and where they are located is essential for assessing software security.
method: The paper presents security feature location as a task and presumably develops a method to map code locations to security features.
result: The task enables developers to understand security implementations and evaluate if intended security properties are enforced.
conclusion: Security feature location provides a basis for analyzing and improving software security.

title: Robust Coverless Linguistic Steganography Via Sentence Embedding Space With Global Resynchronization
authors: Lizhi Xiong, Yuping Lu, Jun Li, Ziqiang Li, Zhangjie Fu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04970v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Linguistic steganography enables covert communication through natural language. Existing methods heavily rely on token-level operations and struggle to maintain reliability under word- and sentence-level textual perturbations. Moreover, variable-length coding-based schemes are highly susceptible to bit-slippage under minor disturbances, as perturbations cause desynchronization between embedded and extracted bit sequences. To address these issues, we propose a robust coverless steganographic framework that operates in the sentence embedding space rather than the token space. Specifically, secret messages are encoded as hierarchical clustering paths in the sentence embedding space, which enhances decoding stability against word- and sentence-level textual perturbations. To tackle the bit-slippage problem, we introduce a Global Resynchronization Mechanism (GRM) that reframes variable-length bitstreams as discrete symbols anchored to semantic subspaces, decoupling local embedding failures from global message recovery. Experimental results demonstrate that under word- and sentence-level perturbations, our approach achieves substantial improvements in robustness, while maintaining effective embedding capacity and exhibiting strong resistance to statistical analysis.
tldr: This paper introduces a coverless linguistic steganography method using sentence embeddings and a global resynchronization mechanism to improve robustness against text perturbations.
motivation: Existing token-level steganography methods are fragile under textual perturbations and suffer from bit-slippage issues. The authors aim to achieve robust covert communication in natural language.
method: Secret messages are encoded as hierarchical clustering paths in sentence embedding space; a Global Resynchronization Mechanism treats variable-length bitstreams as discrete symbols anchored to semantic subspaces to decouple local errors from recovery.
result: Experiments show substantial improvements in robustness under word- and sentence-level perturbations while maintaining embedding capacity and resisting statistical analysis.
conclusion: The proposed approach demonstrates a promising direction for robust coverless steganography, but the work is unrelated to quantum information and its relevant applications.

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning For Optimization Of Star-ris Phase And Energy Splitting Coefficients In Otfs-noma Framework
authors: Rais. J. Gachaba, Manobendu Sarker, Anirban Bhowal
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04536v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper considers a downlink communication framework comprising a simultaneously transmitting and reflecting reconfigurable intelligent surface (STAR-RIS)-aided by orthogonal time frequency space (OTFS) and non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) technologies. Further, delay-Doppler mobility in such frameworks renders classical alternating optimization impractical for per-coherence interval reconfiguration. To mitigate such issues, the STAR-RIS phase-shift and energy-splitting design is formulated as a constrained, non-convex sum-rate maximization problem with closed-form maximum ratio transmission beamforming and fixed NOMA power allocation. To circumvent the per-interval re-optimization burden, a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) approach is adopted that maps observed channel realizations to STAR-RIS configurations through a single forward pass. Specifically, Beta-Space Soft Actor-Critic (SAC-BSE), a maximum entropy DRL agent, is proposed. Simulation results, with two NOMA-multiplexed users on each STAR-RIS branch, confirm rapid convergence, limit the sum-rate degradation to roughly 10\% across a 128-fold user-speed range, and yield consistent gains over OTFS-only, NOMA-only, STAR-RIS-only, fixed-split, and mode-switching baselines as transmit power and the number of STAR-RIS elements increase.
tldr: This paper applies deep reinforcement learning to optimize STAR-RIS phase shifts and energy splitting in an OTFS-NOMA downlink framework.
motivation: Classical alternating optimization is impractical for per-coherence-interval reconfiguration in high-mobility OTFS-NOMA systems, motivating a learning-based approach.
method: The authors formulate a constrained non-convex sum-rate maximization problem and propose Beta-Space Soft Actor-Critic (SAC-BSE), a maximum-entropy DRL agent that maps channel realizations to STAR-RIS configurations in a single forward pass.
result: Simulations with two NOMA users per STAR-RIS branch show rapid convergence, sum-rate degradation limited to ~10% across a wide user-speed range, and consistent gains over various baselines.
conclusion: The DRL approach effectively handles reconfiguration in dynamic OTFS-NOMA environments, outperforming alternative schemes.

title: The History Is The Detector: Executing Cve Patch History, End-to-End
authors: Qiushi Wu, Kevin Eykholt, Youngja Park, Xiaokui Shu, Dhilung Kirat, Douglas Lee Schales, Ian Molloy
abstract: ArXiv:2609.05335v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Public vulnerability databases collect rich information about known software flaws, including their weakness types, affected components, and related patches. Fixing commits provide the exact code changes that removed these flaws. While these records capture why the original code was unsafe, they are documented mainly for human inspection rather than automated reuse. Consequently, the same unsafe conditions may still exist elsewhere in code without a known advisory, leaving much of this detection knowledge unused. We present BUGSTONE-E2E, a framework that transforms vulnerability history into executable detection rules and validates their findings. First, BUGSTONE-E2E mines reusable rules from verified fixing commits, capturing scan anchors, fix semantics, and CVE provenance and organizing them by CWE and language. Second, detection follows a funnel-shaped pipeline: early stages process a large pool of candidates using lightweight analysis, while later stages apply increasingly capable and expensive models to a shrinking set of targets. Specifically, BUGSTONE-E2E first enumerates call sites matching rule anchors using Tree-sitter, then removes benign sites using lightweight heuristics without LLM calls. Next, LLM-based agents inspect the remaining candidates guided by the rule. Following this inspection, the system re-triages surviving candidates and builds runtime verifications, then generates scope-checked patches validated via two-sided differential tests. Using 19,325 high-severity CVEs from 2022 to 2026, BUGSTONE-E2E identifies 2,710 fixing commits and constructs 1,033 detection rules across 56 CWE families, packaged into 172 skills. When applied across 14 programs, it produced runtime evidence for 644 findings. These results demonstrate that CVE history can be turned into an executable workflow, transforming past vulnerabilities into reproducible detection and repair.
tldr: The paper presents BUGSTONE-E2E, a framework that converts CVE patch history into executable detection rules and validates findings through runtime verification.
motivation: Public vulnerability data is documented for humans, not automated reuse, leaving many unsafe code patterns undiscovered.
method: Mines reusable detection rules from fixing commits, uses a funnel-shaped pipeline with lightweight analysis, LLM-based agents, and runtime differential tests.
