result: Identified 2,710 fixing commits, built 1,033 rules, and produced runtime evidence for 644 findings across 14 programs.
conclusion: CVE history can be transformed into an executable workflow for reproducible vulnerability detection and repair.

title: Publish Or Perish: A Population-dynamics Model Of The Corruption Of Peer Review
authors: Shyam Ranganathan
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04443v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Peer review is commonly treated as a mechanism of quality control. This article examines what happens when participants are split between two groups. Explicators assess whether submissions present logic-based arguments (whether deductive, inductive or abductive), independently of whether they agree with the reasons or the conclusion. Interpreters assess submissions according to their outlook. Their employment of logic is opportunistic, as a means of presenting their own views, but not as a means of assessing others' views. Using a deterministic population-dynamics model of iterative games of "Publish or Perish," this article shows how this asymmetry permits interpreters to increase their population share even when they begin as a small minority. It compares fixed and survivor-drawn reviewer panels, alternative replenishment rules, hostile explicator responses, generational differences in ratios, and different panel sizes. Under survivor-drawn review, explicator hostility to interpreters produces an unstable equilibrium at an explicator share of [MATH]: below this threshold, interpreters can survive without explicator cooperation and continue toward dominance. The threshold is not universal, however. Exogenous replenishment in favour of explicators can eliminate the point of no return, and sufficiently lagged, generational replenishment can permit explicators to recover after it has apparently been crossed. The model therefore identifies not only a mechanism by which peer review becomes corrupted, but also the institutional conditions determining whether that corruption becomes self-sustaining or reversible.
tldr: A population-dynamics model of peer review shows how interpreters, who assess based on outlook rather than logic, can dominate explicators even starting as a minority.
motivation: To understand how peer review becomes corrupted when participants have asymmetric assessment criteria.
method: Deterministic population-dynamics model of iterative 'Publish or Perish' games, comparing fixed and survivor-drawn panels, replenishment rules, and panel sizes.
result: Interpreters increase their population share under certain conditions; explicator hostility creates an unstable equilibrium threshold beyond which interpreters dominate.
conclusion: Institutional conditions, such as exogenous or generational replenishment, determine whether corruption becomes self-sustaining or reversible.

title: Reduced Precision Diffusion Synthetic Acceleration For S$_n$ Neutron Transport In LLNL's Ardra Using Hypre
authors: Mario Ivan Ortega Joanna Piper Morgan
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04451v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fast solution times in production discrete ordinates transport codes often require the use of diffusion synthetic acceleration (DSA). A good implementation of DSA will substantially reduce the number of iterations to converge the transport solution at the cost of solving a diffusion-like linear system at each iteration. Often fewer transport iterations will lead to smaller times to solution. Recent work has shown the promise of reduced precision preconditioning. Time and memory cost can be decreased as long as the reduced precision does not substantially degrade the convergence behavior of the higher precision linear system being solved. In this paper, we discuss the algorithmic implications of accelerating transport iterations in double precision (64 bit) while using a reduced precision (32 bit) DSA solve. We initially implement a stand alone code to investigate any theoretical limitations of reduced precision DSA in slabs. Then we implement reduced precision DSA in ARDRA, Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory's (LLNL) discrete ordinance neutral particle transport code, coupled with {\it hypre}, LLNL's scalable linear solver and multigrid methods library capable of mixed precision linear solves Then we solve various neutron transport problems of interest. We find that in most circumstances, DSA acceleration in reduced precision has little to no impact on the acceleration properties of DSA when used with source iteration in most circumstances. However, as tighter tolerances are required, reduced precision DSA may fail to successfully accelerate the transport solve and increase time to solution.
tldr: This paper explores using reduced precision (32-bit) diffusion synthetic acceleration (DSA) to speed up neutron transport simulations in LLNL's ARDRA code, finding it generally effective but unreliable for tight convergence tolerances.
motivation: To reduce computational cost in neutron transport simulations without significantly degrading convergence, by leveraging reduced precision preconditioning.
method: They implemented reduced precision DSA in a standalone slab code and then integrated it into ARDRA using hypre's mixed precision capabilities, testing on various neutron transport problems.
result: Reduced precision DSA had little impact on acceleration properties in most cases, but failed to accelerate convergence when tighter tolerances were required, increasing time to solution.
conclusion: While reduced precision DSA is often beneficial, careful consideration of tolerance requirements is necessary to avoid performance degradation.

title: Frugal Effective Models For Nanophotonic Scattering: Optimizing Global Polarizability Matrices For Metasurface Design
authors: Peter R. Wiecha Sofia Ponomareva
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04863v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate nano-photonics simulations of large scale devices like optical metasurfaces require high accuracy reduced models for the device constituents. We present an automated framework for the optimization of Global Polarizability Matrix (GPM) models, which represent a complex scatterer as a small set of non-local effective dipoles. Our goal is to find the most frugal model that reproduces a particle's scattering response within a user-defined accuracy. The method iteratively removes redundant dipoles while re-adapting the positions of the remaining ones via gradient based optimization, stopping at the smallest model that still meets the target. Automatic differentiation, combined with an untrained neural network that reparametrizes the dipole positions, helps to place the dipoles at physically intuitive locations. We demonstrate the versatility of this approach across diverse geometries, from two dimensional ridges over simple spheres to complex three-dimensional particles, achieving compression factors of typically two orders of magnitude compared to full-wave simulations, for target accuracies in the order of few percent. We finally demonstrate how accurate, frugal effective models enable large-scale meta-deflector optimization without periodic approximations. This robust recipe for constructing frugal effective models paves the way for the rapid simulation of large-scale photonic assemblies, required for example for metasurface design.
tldr: A framework to optimize effective dipole models for nanophotonic scatterers, enabling accelerated simulation of large-scale metasurfaces.
motivation: Accurate simulation of large photonic devices like metasurfaces requires high-fidelity reduced models; current full-wave simulations are computationally expensive.
method: Iteratively removes redundant dipoles and re-adapts their positions via gradient-based optimization, using automatic differentiation and an untrained neural network for parameterization.
result: Achieves compression factors of about two orders of magnitude for diverse geometries while maintaining few percent accuracy, and enables large-scale meta-deflector optimization without periodic approximations.
conclusion: Robust recipe for building frugal effective models, potentially useful for rapid simulation of large photonic assemblies, but not relevant to the specified research areas.

title: Multivariable Extremum Seeking For Locally Lipschitz Objectives
authors: Alan Williams
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04401v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Classical extremum seeking (ES) is commonly interpreted as approximating gradient descent, but this interpretation is less clear for nonsmooth objectives in the continuous-time multivariable setting. We propose a minimal modification of the classical multivariable perturbation--demodulation architecture: rationally independent perturbation frequencies and matched demodulation signals. For any locally Lipschitz static objective, the Kronecker--Weyl theorem shows that, at every fixed perturbation amplitude, the long-time averaged dynamics are exactly the negative gradient of a kernel-smoothed objective. Because rationally independent frequencies render the perturbation and demodulation signals nonperiodic, we employ general averaging theory rather than periodic averaging theory. If the gradient flow of the smoothed objective is globally uniformly asymptotically stable, then the ES dynamics are practically globally uniformly asymptotically stable. We also derive a general matching condition relating the perturbation occupation density, demodulation signal, and smoothing kernel, yielding a family of alternative designs. Numerical examples include a nonsmooth objective function, which may be interpreted as the penalty function of a nonlinear program, and the Rastrigin function, for which smoothing eliminates all undesired local minima.
tldr: This paper proposes a modification to multivariable extremum seeking to handle nonsmooth objective functions using rationally independent perturbation frequencies, showing averaged dynamics are gradient descent on a smoothed objective.
motivation: Classical extremum seeking approximates gradient descent, but this interpretation is unclear for nonsmooth objectives in continuous-time multivariable settings.
method: The authors modify the classical perturbation-demodulation architecture by using rationally independent perturbation frequencies and matched demodulation signals, leveraging general averaging theory via the Kronecker-Weyl theorem.
result: For locally Lipschitz objectives, the long-time averaged dynamics exactly equal the negative gradient of a kernel-smoothed objective, and practical global uniform asymptotic stability is established under a gradient flow assumption. Numerical examples on nonsmooth and Rastrigin functions demonstrate effectiveness.
conclusion: The proposed method extends extremum seeking to nonsmooth objectives, offering a family of designs and confirming that smoothing eliminates undesired local minima.

title: Adaptive Multilevel Discontinuous Galerkin Methods On GPUs
authors: Micha{\l} Wichrowski
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04534v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: I present a matrix-free symmetric interior penalty discontinuous Galerkin method for adaptively refined Cartesian meshes on GPUs. At non-matching interfaces, auxiliary represent the adjacent coarse polynomial on the fine level. This approach converts non-matching interfaces into matching faces, permitting uniform face evaluation throughout the mesh. I prove that this construction is equivalent to the standard non-matching formulation. Furthermore, this representation yields a local geometric multigrid method in which frozen shadows provide inter-level boundary data and carry residual contributions to coarser levels. A primal--dual pairing eliminates shadow assembly from the Krylov iteration. Numerical experiments with cubic elements ([MATH]) on an NVIDIA A100 show stable multigrid convergence under increasing refinement depth and efficient GPU execution.
tldr: This paper presents a GPU-optimized discontinuous Galerkin method for adaptive meshes with a multigrid solver, focusing on numerical PDE simulation.
motivation: The need for efficient high-order numerical methods on adaptive grids for large-scale simulations.
method: Proposes a matrix-free symmetric interior penalty DG method with auxiliary representation for non-matching faces, enabling uniform face evaluation and a local geometric multigrid with frozen shadows.
result: Demonstrates stable multigrid convergence and efficient execution on NVIDIA A100 with cubic elements.
conclusion: The method provides an efficient GPU implementation for adaptive DG, but has no relevance to quantum information or related topics.

title: Fixed Point Theorems For Paired Contractive Mappings In b-Metric Spaces
authors: Hezekiah Seun Adewinbi
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04586v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we introduce the notion of paired-Chatterjea contraction for single-valued mappings in b-metric spaces and establish several fixed point theorems under this contractive condition. We demonstrate that every Chatterjea-type contraction is a paired-Chatterjea contraction, while the converse implication does not hold, thereby showing that the latter class properly extends the former. Additionally, we investigate fixed point results for paired and paired-Kannan contractions in b-metric spaces. Several concrete examples are provided to illustrate the applicability and sharpness of the obtained results. Our findings extend and generalize a number of existing fixed point theorems in the literature.
tldr: Introduces and studies paired-Chatterjea, paired-Kannan, and paired contractions in b-metric spaces, proving fixed point theorems that generalize existing results.
motivation: To extend fixed point theory by introducing more general contraction conditions that include known types as special cases.
method: Defines new contractive conditions and proves existence and uniqueness of fixed points via iterative sequences and the completeness of b-metric spaces.
result: Demonstrates that every Chatterjea contraction is a paired-Chatterjea contraction but not conversely, and provides examples to illustrate applicability and sharpness.
conclusion: Establishes new fixed point theorems that generalize a number of existing results in the literature.

title: Blind Random Search With Noisy Loss Measurements: Averaging, Thresholding, And Almost Sure Convergence
authors: Xintong Jiang Zixian Zhou
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04636v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Blind random search repeatedly draws a candidate point and replaces the current estimate whenever the candidate has a lower loss. In the absence of noise, the true loss is observed directly. It decreases strictly at every accepted update and is monotone nonincreasing over all iterations. Measurement noise can make a worse candidate appear better and thereby break this monotonicity. To recover almost sure convergence under noise, we incorporate averaging and thresholding into the original decision criterion. These two classical tools are coupled. As the sample sizes grow, the positive threshold shrinks at a matched rate. These modifications allow blind random search to recover eventual monotonicity of the true loss under noisy measurements and to converge almost surely.
tldr: This paper proposes modifications to blind random search, namely averaging and thresholding, to recover almost sure convergence when loss measurements are noisy.
motivation: Blind random search is a simple optimization method that relies on comparing loss values, but measurement noise can break monotonicity and prevent convergence; the authors aim to restore convergence guarantees.
method: The authors incorporate averaging of loss measurements and a positive threshold that shrinks as sample sizes grow, showing that these modifications align with the decision criterion to maintain eventual monotonicity.
result: They prove that the modified algorithm converges almost surely to the optimal loss under noisy measurements.
conclusion: The work establishes that averaging and thresholding are effective in ensuring convergence of blind random search in noisy environments.

title: Local Centralizer Rigidity For A Non-generic Diagonal Map
authors: Amie Wilkinson Zhijing Wendy Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04643v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we prove centralizer rigidity for any non-trivial diagonal map in the compact homogeneous space SL_n/\Gamma, n\ge 5, under the assumption that the perturbed volume-preserving diffeomorphism has a regular isomorphic centralizer.
tldr: The paper proves centralizer rigidity for a class of non-generic diagonal maps on the homogeneous space SL_n/Γ, showing that volume-preserving diffeomorphisms with regular isomorphic centralizers are conjugate to the diagonal map.
motivation: To understand rigidity phenomena in smooth dynamical systems, particularly for actions on homogeneous spaces, and to extend results beyond generic assumptions.
method: The proof likely uses tools from smooth ergodic theory, Lie group actions, and analysis of centralizers of diffeomorphisms, possibly using local perturbations and regularity conditions.
result: They prove centralizer rigidity for any non-trivial diagonal map in SL_n/Γ, n≥5, under a regularity assumption on the centralizer.
conclusion: This contributes to the rigidity theory of algebraic actions and may have implications for broader classification problems in smooth dynamics.

title: A Complete Resolution Of Forsythe's Conjecture For Restarted Conjugate Gradients
authors: Matthew J. Colbrook, George Stepaniants, Alex Townsend
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04659v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Forsythe's conjecture, published in 1968, asserts that for each restart length [MATH], every exact-arithmetic restarted conjugate-gradient iteration on a real symmetric positive definite problem either terminates or has normalised residuals that converge separately along the even and odd restart subsequences. Apart from the classical steepest-descent case, this asymptotic question remained unresolved in full generality for nearly six decades. We give a complete classification by restart length in the original finite-dimensional setting and identify a sharp threshold. For [MATH] and [MATH], every problem either terminates or has convergent even and odd residual directions. For every [MATH], there is a diagonal positive definite counterexample of dimension [MATH] which never terminates and whose even residual directions do not converge. Together with Akaike's theorem for [MATH], this shows that the conjectured universal conclusion is true precisely for [MATH] and false for every [MATH]. The positive results follow from a degree-independent double-orthogonality identity and an analysis of the low-degree fixed-point sets. At restart length four, rational interval arithmetic and Sturm sequences certify a transverse Hopf point of the leading vector field of the rescaled squared-weight map. Analytic periodic-orbit and shadowing arguments yield the counterexample at restart length four, and degree elevation extends the construction to every larger restart length.
tldr: This paper resolves Forsythe's conjecture on the convergence of restarted conjugate gradient methods, providing a complete classification by restart length.
motivation: The conjecture about the asymptotic convergence of restarted CG iterations had been unresolved for nearly six decades.
method: The authors use a double-orthogonality identity, fixed-point analysis, rational interval arithmetic, and analytic periodic-orbit arguments.
result: They show that for restart lengths 2 and 3, convergence holds, while for restart length 4 and above, there exist counterexamples with non-converging even residual directions.
conclusion: The conjecture is true precisely for restart lengths 2 and 3 and false for all larger restart lengths.

title: Convex Modeling Of Price Cross-Impact Over Time
authors: Madeleine Udell Vincent Yinjun-Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04712v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Transaction costs can make or break a trading strategy, particularly in relative-value trading of commodity and macro markets, where edges are a few basis points. Price impact is a central component of transaction cost. Price impact models usually include self-impact (a trade in a contract moves that contract's price) but omit two well-documented effects: cross-impact (a trade in one contract also moves the prices of related contracts) and transient impact (price impact decays over time, so an unwind recovers part of the entry cost). A model without these effects overprices the impact of relative-value trades, whose correlated legs are built and unwound over days, and so forgoes potentially profitable trades. This paper models both effects with a convex quadratic cost. In each period, a positive semidefinite matrix built from volatility, volume, and correlation forecasts couples trades across contracts. A power-law decay kernel then couples trades across periods. The resulting cost admits no price manipulation even when liquidity varies over the planning horizon. The model is demonstrated empirically on calendar spread trading of crude oil futures around the commodity index roll.
tldr: This paper presents a convex quadratic model for transaction costs that captures cross-impact and transient impact, demonstrated on crude oil futures calendar spreads.
motivation: In relative-value trading, ignoring cross-impact and transient price impact leads to overestimated transaction costs and missed profitable opportunities.
method: The cost is modeled as a convex quadratic function where a positive semidefinite matrix couples trades across contracts based on volatility, volume, and correlation forecasts, while a power-law decay kernel couples trades across time.
result: The model precludes price manipulation under varying liquidity and is empirically validated on crude oil futures around the index roll.
conclusion: The proposed model provides a practical and theoretically grounded framework for estimating transaction costs in multi-asset trading.

title: The Skew Commutators Of Toeplitz And Hankel Operators In Vector-valued Hardy Space
authors: Santanu Dey Priyanka Aroda
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04752v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this article, we characterize when a Toeplitz operator and a Hankel operator on the vector-valued Hardy space are skew commutators of each other, and determine necessary and sufficient conditions under which their product is self-adjoint. These characterizations extend the results in . In addition, we completely classify the skew commutators of the unilateral shift [MATH], its adjoint [MATH] and [MATH] We also characterize the class of bounded linear operators that have [MATH], [MATH] and [MATH] as skew-commutators.
tldr: This paper characterizes when Toeplitz and Hankel operators on vector-valued Hardy spaces are skew commutators and when their product is self-adjoint.
motivation: To understand structural properties of operators in Hardy spaces, specifically skew commutativity relations and self-adjointness of products, extending prior results.
method: The authors use operator theory and functional analysis techniques to derive necessary and sufficient conditions for the skew commutativity and self-adjointness conditions.
result: They provide complete characterizations for skew commutators and classify cases involving the unilateral shift and its adjoint.
conclusion: The results generalize known theorems and offer a full classification in certain operator classes.

title: Policy Iteration For Domain Randomized Linear Quadratic Systems
authors: Farnaz Adib Yaghmaie Abbas Pasdar
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04794v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this work, we study policy optimization under domain randomization for linear quadratic control, focusing on learning a single state-feedback controller that minimizes the average cost across systems with uncertain dynamics. We propose a policy iteration algorithm with a step-size rule that preserves stability across all sampled systems at each iteration. We show that the method yields monotonic improvement of the sample-average objective and that a stabilizing step size always exists. Under standard smoothness assumptions, the iterates converge subsequentially to stationary points, and under a gradient-dominance condition, we obtain a global linear convergence rate.
tldr: A policy iteration algorithm for domain randomized linear quadratic systems that preserves stability at each step and achieves convergence guarantees.
motivation: To learn a single state-feedback controller robust to uncertain dynamics by minimizing the average cost across a distribution of systems, while ensuring stability throughout the optimization.
method: Proposes a policy iteration scheme with a step-size rule that maintains stability for all sampled systems, and proves monotonic improvement of the sample-average objective.
result: Under standard smoothness assumptions, the iterates converge subsequentially to stationary points; with an additional gradient-dominance condition, global linear convergence is established.
conclusion: Provides a theoretically sound algorithm for domain randomized linear quadratic control with strong convergence properties, but is unrelated to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Construction Of Trace-preserving Fortin Operators
authors: Tabea Tscherpel Franziska Eickmann
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04926v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a unifying framework to construct local Fortin operators for conforming mixed finite element pairs for the Stokes equations. The operators are constructed to satisfy the divergence-preservation property, local stability and approximation properties, and certain trace-preservation properties. For the latter, some of the finite element pairs require an enrichment of the velocity space. We present the construction for the [MATH] element, the Bernardi-Raugel element, the conforming Crouzeix-Raviart element, a modified MINI element and generalised Taylor-Hood elements. Furthermore, we discuss implications of the existence of such a Fortin operator beyond inf-sup stability. These include applications to non-Newtonian fluid flow, problems with inhomogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions, as well as uniform inf-sup stability relevant for domain approximation and moving domains.
tldr: This paper presents a unified framework for constructing local Fortin operators that preserve trace properties for conforming mixed finite element pairs for Stokes equations.
motivation: The need for Fortin operators that satisfy divergence-preservation, stability, and trace-preservation for mixed finite element methods, with applications to non-Newtonian flow and inhomogeneous boundary conditions.
method: They introduce a unifying construction for local Fortin operators, including enrichments for certain velocity spaces, and apply it to several specific element types.
result: The construction yields trace-preserving Fortin operators with the desired properties for multiple finite element pairs, and they discuss implications beyond inf-sup stability.
conclusion: These operators enable improved treatment of non-Newtonian flows, inhomogeneous boundary conditions, and uniform inf-sup stability for domain approximation.

title: Open-Loop Stackelberg Lq Difference Games With Coupled-Affine Inequality Constraints: An Exact Ocp--lcs/lcqp Reformulation
authors: Puduru Viswanadha Reddy Shrestha Ghosh
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04928v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this letter, we study finite-horizon linear-quadratic Stackelberg difference games with coupled-affine state-control inequality constraints. Under the stated assumptions, we show that generalized open-loop Stackelberg equilibria admit an exact reformulation as an optimal control problem subject to a discrete-time linear complementarity system. Eliminating the dynamic variables yields a large-scale linear complementarity quadratic program, together with an explicit recovery map for the follower strategy. This reformulation enables the numerical computation of these equilibria. We illustrate the proposed approach using a constrained network-flow game.
tldr: This paper reformulates finite-horizon linear-quadratic Stackelberg difference games with inequality constraints as an optimal control problem with a linear complementarity system, enabling numerical computation.
motivation: To compute equilibria in constrained Stackelberg games, which are common in economics and control but computationally challenging.
method: The authors prove that under stated assumptions, the generalized open-loop Stackelberg equilibria exactly reformulate as an optimal control problem subject to a discrete-time linear complementarity system. They then eliminate dynamic variables to yield a large-scale linear complementarity quadratic program with an explicit recovery map for the follower strategy.
result: The approach is illustrated on a constrained network-flow game.
conclusion: The reformulation enables numerical computation of these equilibria.

title: Dimension-free $H^\infty$-calculus Of Angle $<\pi/2$ For UMD-valued Ornstein--Uhlenbeck Operators
authors: Jan van Neerven
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04974v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH], let [MATH] be a UMD Banach space, let [MATH], and let [MATH] be the generator of the Ornstein--Uhlenbeck semigroup [MATH] on [MATH]. We prove that the operators [MATH] are [MATH]-sectorial with a common angle strictly smaller than [MATH] and with bounds independent of [MATH]. Combining this with the Hieber--Pr\"uss transference theorem and the Kalton--Weis angle comparison, we deduce that the operators [MATH] admit bounded [MATH]-calculi of a common angle strictly smaller than [MATH], again with dimension-free bounds. The corresponding Walsh [MATH]-analyticity estimates are proved first and transferred to the Ornstein--Uhlenbeck setting by a central limit argument.

motivation: To establish functional calculus and maximal regularity results for Ornstein-Uhlenbeck operators that are independent of the ambient dimension, which is desirable for applications in infinite-dimensional analysis.
method: The proof combines the Hieber-Prüss transference theorem and the Kalton-Weis angle comparison, with Walsh analyticity estimates transferred via a central limit argument.

title: Sarymsakov-Type Semigroups With Support Dominance And Nested Mixing Cores
authors: Shun-Pin Hsu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.05050v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This note develops three multiplication-closed families of stochastic matrices for consensus under arbitrary switching. The first is a support-dominance enlargement of an earlier power-generated construction, in which exact support-pattern matching is relaxed to a dominance-type condition without losing closure under multiplication. The second is a fixed-core class with an exact uniform scrambling horizon and corresponding convergence-rate guarantees for switching products. The third and main contribution is the almost Sarymsakov class, obtained by allowing variable mixing-core dimensions under suitable structural conditions. This new semigroup class properly contains the classical Sarymsakov class and admits a dimension-only scrambling-horizon bound. Examples illustrate the necessity of the proposed structural assumptions and clarify the sharpness or limitations of the derived bounds.
tldr: This paper develops three new classes of stochastic matrices for consensus under arbitrary switching, including an almost Sarymsakov class with dimension-only convergence bounds.
motivation: The study aims to extend the classical Sarymsakov class of stochastic matrices to broader semigroups that guarantee consensus convergence under time-varying communication topologies.
method: The author constructs three multiplication-closed families of stochastic matrices: a support-dominance enlargement, a fixed-core class with scrambling horizon, and the almost Sarymsakov class with variable mixing-core dimensions.
result: The almost Sarymsakov class properly contains the classical Sarymsakov class and provides dimension-only scrambling-horizon bounds, with examples illustrating the necessity and tightness of assumptions.
conclusion: The work contributes to the mathematical theory of consensus algorithms but is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: From Plans To Maps: Nonlocal Regularization Of Optimal Transport
authors: Marcello Carioni, Leonardo Del Grande, Jos\'e A. Iglesias, Hidde Sch\"onberger
abstract: ArXiv:2609.05062v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a nonlocal regularization of optimal transport that bridges Kantorovich and Monge formulations. The regularization penalizes oscillations through an interaction kernel singular near the diagonal. We show that, for sufficiently strong singularities, every finite-energy transport plan is induced by a map, yielding equivalence between the regularized Kantorovich and Monge problems. For fractional kernels, the regularizer reduces to a fractional Sobolev seminorm that can allow jump discontinuities, leading to existence results for broad classes of source and target measures. We derive first-order optimality conditions and analyze the vanishing-regularization limit. The regularized functionals [MATH]-converge to the classical Kantorovich problem, while the first-order [MATH]-limit selects, whenever they exist, finite-energy Monge minimizers with minimal nonlocal energy. When no such minimizer exists, we identify a different asymptotic regime and establish a sharp scaling law in a prototypical mass-splitting example. Finally, after lifting the problem to the product of transport plans, we derive a dual formulation using the cone of copositive functions and propose a fixed-point numerical scheme illustrating the regularization.
tldr: The paper introduces a nonlocal regularization of optimal transport that bridges Kantorovich and Monge formulations via a singular interaction kernel.
motivation: To reconcile the relaxed Kantorovich problem with the more restrictive Monge problem, particularly for existence and regularity of transport maps.
method: The regularization penalizes oscillations using a kernel singular near the diagonal; for fractional kernels it reduces to a fractional Sobolev seminorm, and the analysis includes gamma-convergence, first-order optimality conditions, and a dual formulation via copositive functions.
result: For sufficiently strong singularities, every finite-energy transport plan is induced by a map, yielding equivalence between regularized problems; the functionals gamma-converge to classical Kantorovich, and a numerical fixed-point scheme is provided.
conclusion: The regularization provides a smooth transition between plans and maps, with provable convergence properties, but lies outside the user's research focus on quantum information and related topics.

title: Duality For Stochastic Control With non-Markovian Random Coefficients
authors: Peter Bank, Jannis R. Dause, Filippo de Feo, Peter K. Friz
abstract: ArXiv:2609.05101v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop novel duality methods for stochastic optimal control problems under two sources of randomness and non-Markovian random coefficients adapted to just one of them. The Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation is a second-order backward stochastic partial differential equation. Our duality theory provides an alternative description of the random value function in terms of a suitable pathwise optimal control problem parameterized by the realizations of one of the Brownian motions. This allows us to regain Markovianity using the theory of rough optimal control problems, leading to rough second order HJB equations that we solve in a suitable viscosity sense.
tldr: The paper develops novel duality methods for stochastic optimal control with non-Markovian random coefficients, connecting to rough path theory.
motivation: To handle stochastic control problems with non-Markovian random coefficients, which are not amenable to standard Markovian techniques.
method: It introduces a duality that transforms the problem into a pathwise control problem, enabling the use of rough path theory and viscosity solutions for rough HJB equations.
result: Provides an alternative description of the value function and solves the resulting rough second-order HJB equations in a viscosity sense.
conclusion: Offers a new framework for non-Markovian stochastic control, potentially extending to broader applications.

title: Candidate Comparability Before Promotion: Conditional Validation In Adaptive Network Intrusion Detection
authors: Roberto Fern\'andez-Barrios, Iker Pastor-L\'opez, Amaia Pikatza-Huerga, Pablo Garc\'ia Bringas
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04388v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Adaptive network intrusion detection systems retrain classifiers after drift alarms, but an alarm detects change; it does not establish that a challenger should replace the deployed incumbent. Promotion is security-relevant because it changes the model responsible for subsequent attack detection, and evaluating it has a methodological problem: promotion conclusions may depend on how the challenger was constructed and on how much evidence supports it. We test that dependence on CICIDS2017, UNSW-NB15 and ToN-IoT with self-contained challenger pipelines, nested candidate-size controls, a common-harness comparison of nine update policies, and a final sensitivity confining every exact feature vector to one evaluation, training or probe role. Incumbent-owned frozen preprocessing amplified apparent promotion harm; with self-contained challenger pipelines the mean full-drift harm did not persist. Raising nominal candidate evidence from 512 to 2,000 samples per class improved promotion under pool-constructed progressive drift by +0.53, +1.67 and +0.38 balanced-accuracy points: positive and statistically resolved in all three benchmarks, but materially benchmark-dependent rather than homogeneous, and driven mainly by fewer false positives. Policy conclusions were partially robust: policy ordering changed with candidate comparability, no policy globally dominated, and earlier compatibility statements for a label-free estimator and a calibrated ensemble narrowed. Validation helped evidence-disadvantaged challengers but added no average benefit at parity. Thirteen replays on real, time-ordered traffic showed no net harm from always deploying. Challenger construction and evidence should be controlled, reported and interpreted explicitly when promotion is evaluated.
tldr: This paper examines how the construction and evidence of challenger models affect the evaluation of promotions in adaptive network intrusion detection systems.
motivation: Promotion of new classifiers in adaptive intrusion detection is security-relevant, but evaluation may depend on how the challenger is constructed and the evidence supporting it, which is a methodological problem.
method: They tested this dependence on three datasets using self-contained challenger pipelines, nested candidate-size controls, a common-harness comparison of nine update policies, and a sensitivity analysis confining feature vectors to one role.
result: They found that with self-contained pipelines the mean full-drift harm did not persist, increasing candidate evidence improved promotion under pool-constructed progressive drift, and policy ordering changed with candidate comparability; no policy globally dominated.
conclusion: Challenger construction and evidence should be controlled, reported, and interpreted explicitly when promotion is evaluated.

title: Hoss: Fast Oblivious Semantic Search With Heterogeneous Gpu-cpu-tee Architecture
authors: Jianzhang Du, Weijie Huang, Chenghong Wang, Nicolas Tsagareli, Yukui Luo, Xiaofeng Wang, Zhongshu Gu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04522v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Semantic search is widely deployed in modern AI systems, but protecting both data contents and access patterns remains challenging. The current state-of-the-art system, Compass, achieves oblivious semantic search by building an optimized ORAM over HNSW graphs. However, even with aggressive optimizations, it still incurs large overheads. Closing this performance gap is fundamentally difficult: Compass has already removed most cryptographic overheads, leaving ORAM accesses as the dominant cost, which are constrained by well-known Omega(log N) bandwidth lower bounds. Our key insight is that traditional ORAM overhead stems from the assumption of limited private memory, whereas modern GPU TEEs provide large private memory (Pmem) that blinds internal access patterns (Hunt et al., NSDI '23). This shift opens a new design space. We therefore propose Hoss, a first-of-its-kind oblivious semantic search system with a heterogeneous CPU-GPU TEE architecture that supports fast, scalable search with low cost of ownership. In Hoss, the GPU TEE's large Pmem hosts the hot-path HNSW traversal, while the lower layers of the graph, if they exceed GPU capacity, are offloaded to CPU TEEs. The system invokes oblivious primitives only when accessing these lower layers. The availability of large Pmem also enables new optimization opportunities. For example, Hoss features a host-access ORAM mechanism that goes beyond traditional performance constraints and incorporates several data-dependent optimizations that are not possible in prior designs. We implement a prototype of Hoss and benchmark it against Compass. Our results show that Hoss achieves up to 67x speedup while maintaining high recall, with larger gains at scale.
tldr: A fast oblivious semantic search system using a heterogeneous GPU-CPU TEE architecture.
motivation: Existing oblivious semantic search systems like Compass suffer from large overheads due to ORAM access constraints, limiting scalability and performance.
method: Hoss utilizes the large private memory of modern GPU TEEs to handle hot-path HNSW traversal, offloads lower graph layers to CPU TEEs, and introduces host-access ORAM with data-dependent optimizations.
result: Hoss achieves up to 67x speedup over Compass while maintaining high recall, with gains increasing at scale.
conclusion: The authors demonstrate that GPU TEEs with large private memory enable new design opportunities for efficient oblivious search, significantly outperforming prior approaches.

title: Repeat-After-Me: Black-Box Adaptive Visual Prompt Injection
authors: Sizhe Chen, Yu-Lin Tsai, Ivan Evtimov, Kamalika Chaudhuri, Raluca Ada Popa, David Wagner, Arman Zharmagambetov
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04533v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Prompt injection is widely recognized as a major security threat to AI agents that interact with untrusted external data, such as websites, documents, and emails. Prior work has shown that, in the text domain, black-box prompt injection can achieve near-perfect attack success rates (ASRs). In the image domain, however, existing visual prompt injection methods are substantially less effective in attacking frontier commercial VLMs for materially harmful behavior. Achieving such outputs is hard because it requires a long and/or format-compliant target string, such as a precise, parseable native tool call with exact function names and arguments. We present Repeat-After-Me, a black-box adaptive visual prompt injection attack that can reveal personally identifiable information or make malicious tool calls. Across both open-weight and commercial frontier VLMs, including Qwen3.6-27B and GPT-5.5, our method achieves ASRs exceeding 80% and 47%, respectively, under a realistic setting in which the benign user prompt is semantically unrelated to the injected task and does not verbally authorize it. In our evaluation, injections optimized on one surrogate retain 43-46% of the original ASR on two commercial victims, and cross-sample transferability retains 64-66% of the original ASR on those two models. We test our attack in a real-world OpenClaw agent: in a default OpenClaw Discord deployment, an untrusted user can use a minimally injected image to overwrite TOOLS.md, enabling future sensitive behaviors like remote code execution and secret exfiltration. We show our new attack vector works in cases where adaptive textual prompt injection fails. We discuss potential defenses.
tldr: Repeat-After-Me is a black-box adaptive visual prompt injection attack that achieves high success rates in extracting sensitive information or making malicious tool calls from frontier VLMs.
motivation: Prompt injection is a major security threat to AI agents that interact with untrusted data, and visual prompt injection has been less effective than textual methods.
method: The authors propose a black-box adaptive attack that optimizes images to inject prompts, achieving high attack success rates across open-weight and commercial VLMs.
result: The attack achieves ASRs exceeding 80% on Qwen3.6-27B and 47% on GPT-5.5, with transferability across models and demonstrated real-world impact on an OpenClaw agent.
conclusion: The work shows visual prompt injection can be highly effective, highlighting a new attack vector and suggesting potential defenses.

title: Forgetting Without Restarting: Execution-State Unlearning For Stateful Llm Agents
authors: Chao Yao, Yangbo Wei, Zhen Huang, Junhong Qian, Chenle Chen, Shaoqiang Lu, Chen Wu, Lei He
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04875v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-running LLM agents are stateful: beyond the transcript they accrete compressed summaries, plaintext memory, pending tool plans, and, under every serving API, a KV cache. Yet today's "forget" operations delete a plaintext memory record and stop, leaving every artifact derived from the revoked information intact. We formalize execution-state unlearning: after a forget request, the agent must behave as if it had never observed the target. Modeling the runtime as a deterministic transition system, we prove that the pre-target trajectory prefix is shared with this counterfactual world for free, that the post-target suffix is irreducibly tainted without token-level attribution, and that exact unlearning requires at least [MATH] recomputed transitions, where [MATH] is the target's injection step. Provenance-Guided Selective Replay attains this bound as a cross-layer contract spanning prompt, compressed memory, and cache: a provenance graph locates the injection point, checkpoint restoration reduces to cropping the KV cache, and sanitized replay regenerates the counterfactual suffix. Audited with elicitation, stochastic, and string-free behavioral tests across three agent suites, nine baselines, and three model families, memory deletion leaves leakage unchanged, instruction-based forgetting collapses under elicitation (Leak@probes = 1.00), and source redaction still acts on a revoked preference in 80% of episodes, while selective replay is indistinguishable from a full reset at up to 9x fewer recomputed tokens.
tldr: A framework for removing information from stateful LLM agents so they behave as if they never saw it, using provenance-guided selective replay that clips and regrows only the tainted suffix of execution.
motivation: Long-running agents store summaries, compressed memory, and KV caches derived from input; simply deleting a memory record leaves all downstream artifacts intact.
method: Formalizes the runtime as a deterministic transition system, proves that exact unlearning needs recomputation from the injection step, and implements Provenance-Guided Selective Replay which crops the KV cache at the injection point and regenerates the suffix.
result: Across three agent suites, nine baselines, and three model families, selective replay reaches full-reset behavior at up to 9× fewer recomputed tokens, while memory deletion and instruction-based forgetting leak revoked information.
conclusion: Exact execution-state unlearning is achievable and efficient with provenance tracking and selective replay, but only if the source artifact is redacted at the injection point.

title: Strategic Facility Location In Euclidean Spaces
authors: Kim Thang Nguyen, Lucas Perotin, Bertrand Simon
abstract: ArXiv:2609.05132v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The strategic facility location problem is defined as follows: [MATH] agents report their location in a metric space, and the objective is to design a deciding the (possibly randomized) location of a facility such that agents have no incentive to lie about their position. We focus on the egalitarian cost, which means that the goal of the mechanism is to minimize the expected maximal facility-agent distance. Meanwhile, mechanisms must be (or ): no agent may decrease their expected distance to the facility via lying on their location. Designing truthful mechanisms minimizing the approximation ratio is a well-studied problem, and the optimal solution is known for the real line. We focus in this paper on higher dimension Euclidean spaces, for which gaps remain between the best known lower and upper bounds. We first show that, maybe counter-intuitively, the problem is easier for two agents on the plane rather than on the line: the mechanism can exploit the additional dimension to prevent more efficiently agent lies. Based on this intuition, we devise lower bounds for [MATH] asymptotically matching the best known approximation factor of [MATH] for large [MATH]. We also provide novel mechanism ideas, improving over the best known algorithms on the plane, and when the agents belong to [MATH] but the facility may use an additional dimension.
tldr: Investigates truthful facility location mechanisms in higher-dimensional Euclidean spaces, showing that additional dimensions can help and providing improved approximation bounds.
motivation: The strategic facility location problem asks for a truthful mechanism that minimizes the expected maximal distance, which is optimally solved on the line but not in higher dimensions.
method: The authors analyze the two-agent case on the plane, proving it is easier than on the line, and use this insight to derive lower bounds and propose new mechanisms.
result: They establish lower bounds matching the best known approximation factor asymptotically and present mechanisms that improve over existing algorithms on the plane and when the facility can use an extra dimension.
conclusion: The paper enhances the theory of truthful facility location in Euclidean spaces, demonstrating that additional dimensions can improve truthfulness guarantees.

title: Conformal Prediction For Offensive Security
authors: Giovanni Cherubin
abstract: ArXiv:2609.05165v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Despite its introduction more than a quarter century ago, Conformal Prediction (CP) has seen surprisingly few applications to the cyber security world thus far. In particular, we observe that, while CP has been employed as a defensive measure in many recent works, its use for carrying out attacks (i.e., for offensive security) is hard to trace in the literature. We explore this gap, by presenting initial findings in two key areas of offensive security: Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning, and network traffic analysis.
tldr: This paper explores the underutilized application of Conformal Prediction (CP) for offensive security tasks, specifically privacy-preserving machine learning and network traffic analysis, presenting initial findings in these areas.
motivation: Conformal Prediction has been used mainly for defensive security measures, but its potential for offensive attacks remains largely unexplored. The paper aims to bridge this gap by identifying opportunities where CP can be leveraged in offensive contexts.
method: The authors present preliminary work in two key areas: Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning (where CP could be used to exploit information leaks) and network traffic analysis (where CP might aid in adversarial tasks). They provide initial findings and demonstrate the feasibility of applying CP in these offensive security settings.
result: The paper reports initial success in using CP for offensive purposes, suggesting that it can effectively quantify uncertainty and provide valid prediction sets in attacks, which could be useful for evading detection or exploiting vulnerabilities.
conclusion: The work fills a notable gap in the literature by showing that Conformal Prediction can be adapted for offensive security, opening new research directions in cyber security. However, the findings are preliminary and require further exploration.

title: Hatebench In The Era Of Safer LLMs
authors: Ole Becker, Tobias Jongen, Philip Kolbe, Sonal Khosla, Vaibhav Bajpai
abstract: ArXiv:2609.05169v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) lower the barrier for au- tomated content generation, the potential for producing hate speech poses a significant challenge for digital safety. This paper presents a reproducibility study of the HateBench paper by Shen et al., investigating whether existing hate speech detectors, typically trained on human-authored data, generalize to LLM-generated hateful content, and evaluating whether their reported weaknesses are stable over time and robust to evolving components. We independently reconstruct the original dataset genera- tion pipeline using modern LLMs and extend the benchmark to include recently released models and updated detector versions. Our independent assessment under current con- ditions finds that for newer LLMs, safeguards have been put into place to prevent the generation of harmful content. We also replicate the results for two sophisticated types of hate campaigns. While the original findings seem to have been overestimated slightly due to bias in the datasets, the overall findings can be confirmed. Finally, we compare text- Moderation against the newer omni-Moderation and find that its robustness against adversarial hate campaigns has improved slightly. By clarifying which detector vulnerabil- ities persist, this study informs the community about the longevity of content moderation measurements.
tldr: This paper reproduces and extends a hate speech detection benchmark to assess the generalization and robustness of detectors against LLM-generated hate content.
motivation: To verify whether findings from the original HateBench study, which showed detectors trained on human-authored data fail on LLM-generated hate, still hold with newer models and safeguards.
method: They independently reconstruct the dataset generation pipeline using modern LLMs, extend the benchmark with recent models and updated detectors, and compare text-Moderation and omni-Moderation.
result: They find that newer LLMs have safeguards preventing harmful content generation, replicate results for two hate campaign types but note the original findings were slightly overestimated due to dataset bias, and omni-Moderation shows slightly improved robustness.
conclusion: The study clarifies which detector vulnerabilities persist and informs about the longevity of content moderation measurements.

title: Latency-Optimal Geo-Distributed Storage Over Structured Networks
authors: Viveck Cadambe Madhura Pathegama
abstract: ArXiv:2609.05229v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study latency-optimal file assignment in geo-distributed storage systems modeled as weighted graphs, where edge weights represent communication delays and each node stores one (possibly coded) file. Our goal is to minimize the average time required to retrieve an original file, taken uniformly over all nodes and files. We show that for every fixed number of files [MATH], computing a latency-minimizing assignment is NP-hard via a reduction from the domatic number problem. On the positive side, we identify natural network topologies that admit uncoded, structured optimal assignments in which, for every node, one can choose its [MATH] closest nodes, including itself, so that they store distinct original files. We prove that every weighted tree, certain weighted cycles, and unit-weight graphs with sufficiently large minimum degree admit such assignments. For these graph classes, we provide efficient algorithms to construct latency-optimal file assignments.
tldr: This paper studies latency-optimal file assignment in geo-distributed storage systems, proving NP-hardness for general graphs and presenting efficient algorithms for structured networks.
motivation: To minimize average retrieval time in geo-distributed storage, a practical problem in distributed systems.
method: Formulates the problem on weighted graphs, reduces from domatic number to show NP-hardness, and identifies graph classes (trees, cycles, high-degree unit-weight) with structured optimal assignments, providing constructive algorithms.
result: General problem is NP-hard; polynomial-time solutions exist for certain topologies such as trees and some cycles.
conclusion: The work is unrelated to quantum information or any of the specified research directions, falling under general distributed systems optimization.

title: Continuity: Security-Context Contracts For Composable Llm Agent Controls
authors: Geng Yang Chris Zheng
abstract: ArXiv:2609.05269v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agent systems increasingly combine provenance tracking, authorization, policy enforcement, protocol adapters, and execution controls. However, individually correct security mechanisms do not necessarily compose into an end-to-end secure system: security-critical context may be dropped, widened, rebound, or reinterpreted as actions cross component boundaries. We identify this failure mode as security-context discontinuity and introduce CONTINUITY, a framework for verifiable composition of agent security controls. CONTINUITY models each component with an assume-guarantee contract and carries authenticated security context across transitions using signed root grants, provenance commitments, role-bound transition receipts, bounded typed releases, transformation witnesses, and effect-bound execution permits. We formalize end-to-end consequence integrity, requiring every realized external effect to be backed by a valid and current authorization witness linking the principal, task, provenance, delegation, policy state, canonical action, and finality boundary. We implement a reference verifier and deterministic cross-layer fault-injection suite covering 32 fault classes across four application domains. In 2,560 parameterized attack instances spanning 128 fault-domain classes, the full CONTINUITY configuration commits no harmful external effect, while completing all 700 benign tasks and escalating all 200 ambiguous cases. These results show that secure agent execution requires not only sound individual controls, but explicit contracts that preserve their guarantees across the complete instruction-to-effect path.
tldr: Introduces CONTINUITY, a framework for verifiable composition of security controls in LLM agent systems, addressing security-context discontinuity.
motivation: Individually correct security mechanisms do not necessarily compose into end-to-end secure LLM agent systems due to dropped or reinterpreted security context across component boundaries.
method: Models each component with assume-guarantee contracts, carries authenticated security context via signed grants, provenance commitments, role-bound transition receipts, bounded releases, transformation witnesses, and effect-bound execution permits; implements a reference verifier and fault-injection suite.
result: In 2,560 parameterized attack instances across 128 fault-domain classes, the full configuration commits no harmful external effect while completing all benign tasks and escalating ambiguous cases.
conclusion: Secure agent execution requires explicit contracts that preserve guarantees across the complete instruction-to-effect path.

title: When Llm Decompilers Recompile More And Preserve Less
authors: Chang Liu, Edward Raff, Kristopher Micinski
abstract: ArXiv:2609.05370v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Decompilation recovers high-level source from compiled machine code and serves as a foundation for security tasks such as vulnerability detection and malware analysis. Traditional decompilers like Ghidra and Hex-Rays expose whatever they cannot resolve as visible placeholders and often emit pseudocode that will not compile or execute; LLM-based decompilers produce clean, idiomatic C and are now judged almost entirely by recompilability and re-executability: whether the output builds and passes its shipped input/output tests. We show that these metrics can reward the wrong path: a function may recompile and pass every shipped test yet diverge on other legitimate inputs, and a disclosed vulnerability may disappear from the recompiled code with no visible trace of the crash. Neither failure is caught by existing suites. To address this gap, we propose Decompile-Diverge, a behavioral comparison oracle not relying on fixed or hand-crafted tests: for each function it synthesizes a driver, grows a fuzzing corpus from the reference, and reruns the decompiled code on the same inputs to detect changes in the function's behavior. Across eight systems in nine configurations on established LLM decompilation corpora, candidates that pass every shipped test still diverge from the original on our input corpus: 4.9% overall, and as many as 13% for a single system. On 300 real GitHub library functions and 287 CVE-grounded functions, recompilability and behavioral agreement can come apart: the strongest refinement LLM lifts Ghidra's build rate from 75% to 90%, while its Matched rate falls from 74% to 62%; on disclosed vulnerabilities, up to one tenth exhibit Crash Absence in its output. Source-level analysis traces this divergence to introduced fields, types, callees, and guards that replace the visible unknowns traditional tools leave behind.
tldr: This paper proposes Decompile-Diverge, a behavioral comparison oracle for evaluating LLM-based decompilers, showing that recompilability metrics can miss behavioral divergences and discovered vulnerabilities vanishing.
motivation: Traditional decompilers leave placeholders, while LLM-based decompilers are judged by recompilability and test passing, which can reward the wrong path and miss divergences on other inputs or loss of vulnerabilities.
method: Decompile-Diverge synthesizes a driver for each function, grows a fuzzing corpus from the reference, and reruns decompiled code on the same inputs to detect behavioral changes.
result: Across eight systems in nine configurations, candidates passing shipped tests still diverge on 4.9% overall (up to 13% for a single system); on real GitHub functions and CVE-grounded functions, recompilability and behavioral agreement can conflict, and up to 10% of vulnerabilities exhibit Crash Absence.
conclusion: The paper highlights the inadequacy of existing evaluation metrics for LLM decompilers and proposes a method to detect behavioral divergence, urging more robust evaluation.

title: Ber-pef: Unified Human Mobility Predictability Evaluation Via Bayes Error Rate Estimation
authors: En Xu, Jingtao Ding, Zhiwen Yu, Yong Li
abstract: ArXiv:2609.04292v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Human mobility predictability concerns the best prediction performance attainable from a given target and input information, but its ground truth is not directly observable on real mobility data. We present BER-PEF, a Bayes-error-rate-based framework that converts BER estimation into mobility predictability estimation and provides a unified protocol for comparing estimators without observable ground truth. The framework maps symbolic sequences, numeric trajectories, contextual features, and learned representations into a common feature--label space, then evaluates estimator outputs along controlled perturbation curves against a shared predictability reference interval by measuring deviations below the interval, above the interval, and across the full interval. Experiments on Foursquare NYC and TKY, GeoLife, and T-Drive show that several BER-based estimators achieve lower reference discrepancy than existing predictability methods on symbolic sequences and numeric trajectories, while their estimates track changes in empirical prediction performance under perturbation. Additional analyses show that contextual inputs and multiple structured representations can be evaluated under the same protocol, and that aggregating evidence across multiple perturbation levels provides a more reliable basis for estimator selection than relying on a single unperturbed observation. BER-PEF therefore offers a unified and verifiable path for evaluating predictability estimators on heterogeneous mobility data when ground-truth predictability is unavailable.
tldr: This paper introduces a framework for evaluating human mobility predictability estimators using Bayes error rate estimation without observable ground truth.
motivation: The ground truth for human mobility predictability is not directly observable, making it difficult to compare and evaluate different estimators on real data.
method: The framework maps symbolic sequences, numeric trajectories, contextual features, and learned representations into a common feature-label space, then evaluates estimators along controlled perturbation curves against a shared predictability reference interval.
result: Experiments on several datasets (Foursquare NYC/TKY, GeoLife, T-Drive) show that BER-based estimators achieve lower reference discrepancy than existing methods, and the protocol supports unified evaluation across heterogeneous inputs.
conclusion: The proposed framework offers a unified and verifiable method for comparing predictability estimators on heterogeneous mobility data when ground-truth is unavailable.
